Chapter 6 
 
EXAMINING, PREPARING, AND COUNTING  
VOTED OPTICAL/ DIGITAL SCAN BALLOTS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

 
61 
PROCESSING BALLOTS COUNTED AT CCS 
 
STEP 1 
The early voting clerk must deliver the early voting ballots to the CCS. This should include 
the container for the early voting electronic system ballots that are to be counted by 
automatic tabulating equipment at a CCS. This must be done without opening t he 
container.17 
STEP 2 
The early voting electronic system ballots counted at a CCS, the ballots cast at precinct 
polling places and the ballots voted by mail must be tabulated separately and must be 
separately reported on returns.  
STEP 3 The general custodian of records must post a guard to ensure the security of ballot boxes 
containing voted ballots throughout the period of tabulation at the CCS.  
STEP 4 
The general custodian of election records in a county with a population of 100,000 or more 
must implement a video surveillance system that retains a record of all areas containing 
voted ballots from the time the voted ballots are delivered to the CCS  until the canvass of 
precinct election returns. The surveillance system must also retain a record of all areas 
containing voted ballots from the time the voted ballots are delivered to the SVC  or EVBB 
until the canvass of precinct election returns. The video must be made available to the public 
by a livestream. The recorded video is an electio n record and must be retained by the 
general custodian of election records until the end of the calendar year in which the election 
is held or an election contest filed in the county has been resolved, whichever is later. 
 
[Secs. 87.103, 127.1232] 
 
DELIVERY OF BALLOT BOX 
Poll watchers are entitled to observe the delivery of ballot containers in their own vehicle. While judges 
should facilitate this observation, a watcher does not need to follow the transfer of election materials for 
the delivery to be valid. Upon reaching the CCS, present the ballot box to the CCS presiding judge (or their 
designee) and exchange for a signed receipt. Remind any accompanying watchers that they must have a 
valid Certificate of Appointment of Poll Watcher (Form 4-26, 4-27, 4-28, or 4- 29) and Certificate of 
Completion of Poll Watcher Training administered by the SOS assigning the watcher to the CCS in o rder 
to continue to observe activities after delivery of the ballot containers. Once delivery is complete, ensure 
that all rejected envelopes, jacket envelopes containing the carrier envelopes, and any unused supplies 
are returned to the general custodian of election records. 
 
[Secs. 33.060, 127.068(a), 127.124] 
 
  
                                                           
17 If the ballots are to be delivered to the central counting station before the time the polls are closed on election day, the intervals during the 
day at which the ballots are to be delivered must be stated in the resolution, order, or other official action authorizing the early deliveries. 
  
62 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Chapter 7 
 
RECONVENING EVBB 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

 
63 
The EVBB must reconvene after the election to review and qualify provisional ballots and to qualify ballots 
that were cast from outside the United States on or before election day and that are received by the sixth 
day after election day. The early voting clerk may determine whether or not the SVC will need to 
reconvene after election day to verify signatures or leave that authority with the EVBB . The SOS 
recommends that this decision be made prior to election day. If the authority is left with the SVC, it is 
recommended that the SVC coordinate with the EVBB and the early voting clerk for delivery of the jacket 
envelope ballots by mail. If there is an  SVC, the SVC must verify the signatures before the EVBB meets. 
The SVC would follow the same procedures of when they first convene.  
 
MAY EVBB MEMBERS SERVE ON THE SVC? Not recommended. Since the EVBB members may 
override a rejected signature decision by the committee, an EVBB member should not serve on 
the SVC. 
 
RECONVENING TO REVIEW PROVISIONAL BALLOTS 
The authority appointing the EVBB may determine which members will review and count the provisional 
ballots. The entire EVBB is not required to be present; however, a minimum of three members is required 
to conduct the review.  
 
1. Convening the EVBB 
a. The presiding judge may convene the EVBB as soon as practicable after the voter registrar 
has completed the review of the provisional ballots, or if the voter registrar reviews the 
provisional ballots in “batches” and releases completed “ batches” sequentially, the 
presiding judge may convene the EVBB as soon as practicable after the voter registrar has 
completed one or more “ batches.” The judge must post a notice on the bulletin board  
used for posting notices of meetings of the governing body ordering the election no later 
than 24 hours before each time the EVBB is scheduled to meet. The EVBB may also 
convene while the voter registrar continues the review. 
b. The EVBB cannot convene a final time until the seventh day after the election due to voter 
identification verification and mail ballots subject to corrective action. The SOS 
recommends reviewing provisional ballots on a rolling basis.  
2. Delivery of materials to the EVBB 
a. The EVBB should obtain from the authority conducting the election a package of supplies, 
including the: 
i. Return Sheets; 
ii. Tally Sheets; and 
iii. Envelopes for Accepted and Rejected Ballots.
b. The general custodian will deliver to the EVBB  the Early Voting List of Provisional Voters 
from each precinct. 
3. Delivery of provisional ballots 
a. The EVBB presiding judge must take receipt of the provisional ballots directly from the 
voter registrar or the  general custodian of election records; and the  Early Voting List of 
Provisional Voters at a time and place to be determined by the presiding judge.  
 

  
64 
b. The EVBB presiding judge completes the  Verification of Provisional Ballots and Serial 
Numbers (Form 9-7) by signing at the time of receipt that the seal(s) were intact, serial 
numbers accurately reflected, and number of provisional ballots received. 
4. Review of provisional ballots 
a. The EVBB must examine the notations from both the election judge and voter registrar 
located on the Affidavit of Provisional Voters. Use the following table to decide whether 
a ballot should be counted or rejected.

being photographed and identification

65 
5. Disposition of accepted or rejected ballots 
a. The EVBB presiding judge must record the disposition of each ballot on both the Affidavit 
of Provisional Voter and the Early Voting List of Provisional Voters for that precinct. 
b. Ballots to be counted must be removed from their  Affidavit of Provisional Voter 
envelopes, remaining sealed within their secrecy envelopes. The SOS recommends as a 
best practice that at least 10 secrecy envelopes be accumulated in a separate container 
before they are opened and the ballots counted under the normal procedure for counting 
ballots by mail in an election either by hand counting or by CCS. See Chapter 5 and Chapter 
6 of this handbook for specific counting rules. The EVBB or CCS presiding judge must then 
complete a return sheet of the votes and record them by precinct. The processed Affidavit 
of Provisional Voter envelopes are placed in the Envelope for Provisional Ballot Affidavit 
Envelopes and delivered to the general custodian of election records. 
c. The Affidavit of Provisional Voter envelopes for ballots that are not counted are placed in 
the Envelope for Rejected Early Voting Ballots and delivered to the general custodian of 
election records. 
d. Rejected Affidavit of Provisional Voter envelopes may not be opened except by court 
order.  
6. Counting paper ballot provisional ballots 
a. See Chapter 5 and Chapter 6 of this handbook for specific counting rules. 
b. Once counted, the provisional ballots must be re-locked and returned to the custodian of 
election records. The key must be delivered to the custodian of the key. 
7. Counting of provisional ballots electronically (optical scan) 
a. The CCS manager must decide whether the EVBB  must manually count the ballots with 
the totals manually added to the computer count for a canvass total or whether the CCS 
must reconvene. 
b. The CCS manager must send notice to the EVBB presiding judge prior to reconvening the 
EVBB as to whether the ballots are to be counted manually by the EVBB or whether the 
ballots are to be prepared for delivery to the CCS. 
c. If the ballots are to be counted by the CCS, the manager must post notice at least 24 hours 
prior to reconvening the CCS. Section 1.006 does not apply. 
d. A ballot transmittal form must be completed by the EVBB presiding judge. The transmittal 
form will accompany the accepted provisional ballots. 
e. Prior to the beginning of the count at a CCS , the manager must run the required second 
logic and accuracy test using the same test deck as on election day. a fter the count is 
complete, the manager must run the required third logic and accuracy test. If the test is 
not successful, the count is void. 
f. The CCS manager may add the provisional ballots to the original returns by hand in order 
to provide one complete Return Sheet; may enter the provisional ballots directly on the 
electronic voting system to have one final electronic return sheet ; or may provide a 
separate return sheet with just provisional ballot vote totals. The return sheets are placed 
in Envelope No. 2 and delivered to the custodian of election records. 
  
66 
g. The counted provisional ballots and other election materials are returned to the 
custodian of election records and retained for the 22-month preservation period for that 
election.18 
8. Notice to provisional voters 
a. Within 10 days following the local canvass, the EVBB presiding judge must deliver the 
Notice of Outcome to Provisional Voter  (Form 9-9), informing the voter whe ther their 
ballot was counted and the specific reason for any rejection. The presiding judge must 
use the mailing address provided on the front of the Affidavit of Provisional Voter and 
record the action of the EVBB and sign on the reverse side of the affidavit. 
9. Distribution of provisional voting records 
a. Custodian of election records receives: 
i. Early Voting List of Provisional Voters (Form 9-3) 
ii. Return Sheets (Form 11-7); 
iii. Tally Sheets (Form 11-6); 
iv. Envelope for Provisional Ballot Affidavit Envelopes (Form 7-83); 
v. Envelope for Rejected Early Voting Ballots (Form 10-23); 
vi. Counted ballots; and 
vii. Verification of Provisional Ballots and Serial Numbers (Form 9-7). 
b. Custodian of the key receives: 
i. Key to the ballot box after it has been locked. 
c. Presiding officer of the canvassing authority receives: 
i. Return Sheets (Form 11-7); and 
ii. Tally Sheets (Form 11-6). 
 
[Sec. 65.0541; 1 TAC 81.176(c)(14)] 
 
RECONVENING FOR LATE ARRIVING BALLOTS BY MAIL 
1. The EVBB must reconvene to count mail ballots which: 
a. Arrived by 5 p.m. on the day after election and bear a cancellation mark of a common or 
contract carrier or courier indicating a time no later than 7  p.m. at the location of the 
election on election day; 
b. Were cast from outside the United States; 
c. Were placed in delivery before the polls closed; and 
d. Arrived no later than the fifth day (non -military overseas) or sixth day (military) after 
election day.19 
2. Reconvening the EVBB 
a. The general rule is on the ninth day after election day or earlier, if the early voting clerk 
can determine that all ballots cast from outside the United States have been received. 
b. For a general election for state and county officers, the date moves to the 13th day after 
election day, or earlier if the early voting clerk can determine that all ballots cast from 
outside the United States have been received.  
                                                           
18 Since provisional ballots will probably be processed and counted at the same time as the late early voting by mail ballots, additional procedures relating 
to late ballots pursuant to 1 TAC 81.37 may also apply. 
19 If the fifth or sixth day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal or state holiday, this deadline is extended to the next regular business day.  
 
67 
3. The carrier envelope must be:  
a. Timely submitted; 
b. Properly addressed with postage (no postage is required for FPCA carrier envelopes); and 
c. Bear a cancellation mark from a postal service before the polls close or a receipt mark 
from a common or contract carrier indicating the ballot was received before the polls 
closed.  
 
PROVISIONS RELATED TO EVBB 
Reconvening 
1. The EVBB presiding judge must notify the early voting clerk as to the time and place where the  
EVBB will reconvene. The notice must be made in time so th at the early voting clerk may give 
proper notice of the delivery.  The early voting clerk must post notice of delivery of jacket 
envelopes and any other accompanying papers to the EVBB at least 24 hours prior to the delivery. 
The notice must be posted at the main early voting polling place. Section 1.006 does not apply. 
2. The EVBB presiding judge must send notice to the custodian of the key and the custodian of 
election records to redeliver the ballot box containing the counted ballots and the key to the box. 
After the late ballots have been counted, the presiding judge must lock the late counted ballots 
in the ballot box.  The presiding judge must  deliver the ballot box to the general custodian of 
election records and the key to the ballot box to the custodian of the key. 
3. Poll watchers are entitled to be present. 
4. If all mail ballots were received by the close of voting on election day or no ballots were received 
by the appropriate deadline for the election, the early voting clerk must certify that fact and 
deliver the certification to the canvassing board before they convene to canvass the votes.  
 
Paper Ballots 
1. Once the ballots have been qualified,  the EVBB presiding judge must use the regular method of 
counting ballots by keeping three new tally sheets, counting by precinct, and having at least two 
members per tally team. 
2. Once the EVBB has counted all the ballots, an original and three copies of the return sheet must  
be prepared. 
3. The distribution of the tally sheets and return sheets must be made in accordance with the 
Subchapter B, Chapter 66. 
4. The canvassing board must add the returns from both early voting return sheets when canvassing 
the vote. 
 
Electronic Voting Systems 
1. The CCS manager must decide whether the EVBB must manually count the ballots with the totals 
manually added to the computer count for a canvass total or whether the CCS must reconvene. 
2. Before the EVBB reconvenes, the CCS manager must provide notice to the presiding judge 
regarding the ballot handling method: manual counting by the EVBB or delivery to the CCS. 
3. If the ballots are to be counted by the CCS, the manager must post notice at least 24 hours prior 
to reconvening the CCS. Section 1.006 does not apply. 
4. A ballot transmittal form must be completed by the EVBB presiding judge. The transmittal form 
will accompany the ballots qualified. 
  
68 
5. The manager must order a second test to be conducted prior to the count.  The test must be 
successful. 
6. Poll watchers are entitled to be present. 
7. After the second test is successful, the unofficial election results preserved by electronic means 
must be loaded in the tabulating equipment. 
8. The tabulation supervisor must print a status report before the count is to begin. This status report 
must be compared with the report run on election night. If the two status reports do not match, 
the electronic ballots must be counted by hand and the tot al manually added to the returns 
printed on election night. 
9. If the status reports match, the tabulation supervisor may order the count to begin. The precinct 
returns from these counts may be included with the original precinct counts.  The tabulation 
supervisor does not need to keep the precinct-by-precinct results of the late ballots separate from 
other early voted ballots. 
10. Once the ballots have been counted, results must be prepared in the regular manner.  The 
manager must prepare a certification and attach it to the returns, then place both in envelope #1 
to be delivered to the presiding officer of the canvassing board indicating that the results 
supersede any returns printed prior to the reconvening of the CCS after election day. 
11. After the results have been prepared, a successful third test must be performed. 
12. The results, ballots, and distribution of ballots and all records must  be made in the regular 
manner. 
 
[Secs. 65.001, 86.007, 87.062, 87.103, 87.125; 1 TAC 81.37] 
 
RECONVENING TO REVIE W BALLOTS THAT WERE ELIGIBLE FOR 
CORRECTIVE ACTION 
The EVBB must reconvene on or after the seventh day after election day to review mail ballots that were 
subject to the corrective action process. Since a voter has until the sixth day after election day to correct 
the defect(s), the voter ’s ballot may not be finally rejected for the reason provided in the Notice of 
Defective Carrier Issued by Signature Verification Committee or Early Voting Ballot Board  before the 
seventh day after election day. See Chapter 4 of this handbook for more details.  
 
[Sec. 87.0411(g)] 
 
RECONVENING TO CONDUCT THE POST-ELECTION HAND COUNT AUDIT 
For the general election for state and county officers, the primary election and primary runoff election, or 
an election on a proposed amendment to the constitution or other statewide measure submitted by the 
Legislature, the SOS will select the polling locations and precincts to be counted and designate not more 
than three offices or not more than three propositions to be audited. For all other elections not previously 
referenced, including elections for local political subdivisions , the general custodian of election records 
must conduct an a udit of all races in at least one percent of the early voting polling lo cations and one 
percent of the election day polling locations, or in three early voting polling locations and three election 
day polling locations, whichever is greater, in which an electronic voting system was used. 
 
69 
For precincts in which ballots by mail were received, the Post-Election Hand Count Audit will include one 
percent of the precincts, or three precincts, whichever is greater, in which the ballots were counted with 
a precinct scanner or a central count scanner.  
 
The general custodian of election records must begin the audit no later than 72 hours after the polls close. 
The audit must be completed no later than the 21st day after election day.  No later than the third day 
after the date the a udit is completed, the general custodian of election reco rds must deliver a written 
report of the count to the SOS and post the results of the audit on the county’s website where the county 
posts election results. If a local political subdivision conducts its own election, the SOS recommends the 
local political subdivision post the audit results on its website in the same location that election results 
are posted. 
 
The general custodian of election records must designate the members of the EVBB for the election to 
perform the Post-Election Hand Count Audit at the custodian’s direction. If one or more members of the 
EVBB are unable to serve for the audit, then additional members may be appointed. 
 
Each person who is entitled to appoint watchers in the election is entitled to be present at the Post-
Election Hand Count Audit and is entitled to have a poll watcher present. A watcher appointed to the audit 
must meet the same eligibility requirements and be appointed in the same manner as a watcher under 
Chapter 33. A watcher for the audit must deliver his or her valid Certificate of Appointment of Poll Watcher 
(Form 4-26, 4-27, 4-28, or 4-29) and Certificate of Completion of Po ll Watcher Training administered by 
the SOS to the EVBB presiding judge.  
 
See the Post-Election Hand Count Audit Guide for additional information.  
 
[Sec. 127.201]

Chapter 8 
 
POLL WATCHERS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

73 
A poll watcher appointed to serve at a meeting place for the EVBB may be present at any time the EVBB 
meets to process early voting results until the election officers complete their duties. This chapter 
addresses the authority and rights of poll watchers at the EVBB and the procedures for the acceptance of 
watchers. 
ACCEPTANCE AND QUALIFICATION 
A poll watcher who is appointed to serve must present a valid Certificate of Appointment of Poll Watcher 
(Form 4-26, 4-27, 4-28, or 4-29) and Certificate of Completion of Poll Watcher Training administered by 
the SOS to the EVBB presiding judge when the watcher reports for service. The certificates provided by 
the watcher must be retained with the records of the EVBB. The presiding judge must require the watcher 
to countersign the Certificate of Appointment of Poll Watcher to ensure that the watcher is the same 
person who signed the Certificate of Appointment of Poll Watcher. 
A watcher may not be accepted for service if the watcher has possession of a device capable of recording 
images or sound unless the watcher agrees to disable or deactivate the device. The EVBB presiding judge 
may inquire whether a watcher has possession of any prohibited recording device before accepting the 
watcher for service. 
A watcher who presents himself or herself with the required certificates at the proper time must be 
accepted for service unless the person is ineligible to serve, the watcher refu ses to disable or deactivate 
a prohibited recording device, or the number of watchers to which the appointing authority is entitled 
have already been accepted. If the watcher is not accepted for service, the certificates must be returned 
to the watcher with a signed, written statement of the reason for the rejection. 
Maximum Number of Poll Watchers 
EVBB, CCS, or 
Election Day Polling Place 
A maximum of two watchers may be appointed 
for each location by each appointing authority 

  
74 
Oath  
Before accepting a watcher for service, the presiding judge must require the watcher to take following 
oath administered by an election officer. The oath is found on the Certificate of Appointment of Poll 
Watcher (Form 4-26, 4-27, 4-28, or 4-29):  
 
“I swear (or affirm) that I will not disrupt the voting process or harass voters in the 
discharge of my duties.”  
 
Identification 
If the watcher is accepted for service, an election officer will provide the watcher with a form of 
identification that must be worn by the watcher in the EVBB.20 
 
 
 
 
 
[Sec. 33.051]

A Poll Watcher Must A Poll Watcher May

certificate of completion of poll watcher training 
administered by the SOS. 
Follow the transfer of election materials to the 
EVBB. 
Turn off any recording device while serving as a 
poll watcher. 
Not be prohibited  from making written notes 
while on duty. 
Wear identification  provided by an election 
officer while serving at the EVBB. 
Sit or stand near enough  to provide meaningful 
observation by seeing and hearing the election 
officers conducting the observed activity. Not be disruptive during the qualifying process. 
Be permitted to observe any activity occurring at 
the location at which the watcher is serving. 
Not be denied free movement where election 
activity is occurring within the location at which 
the watcher is serving. 
                                                           
20 Visit the Secretary of State’s Elections Form Index for other sample badges. 
Name Badge for Poll Watchers  
(Form 7-6) 
 
 
75 
A Poll Watcher Must A Poll Watcher May 
Be permitted to inspect election records prepared 
by the election officers at the location where the 
watcher is serving. This includes observing the 
ballot-qualifying process and reviewing logs or 
returns created by the EVBB. 
Call the attention  of an election officer to an 
occurrence that the watcher believes to be an 
irregularity or violation of law. The officer may 
refer the matter to the presiding judge.  
 
Preventing a watcher from observing any activity or procedure the person knows the watcher is entitled 
to observe is a Class A misdemeanor. See the Poll Watcher’s Guide for additional information. 
 
[Secs. 33.055, 33.056, 33.058, 33.061; 1 TAC 81.62] 
 
DISRUPTIONS TO THE EVBB 
While a poll watcher is entitled to observe any activity conducted at the location the watcher is serving, 
they must not disrupt the qualifying process. The  EVBB presiding judge is responsible for maintaining 
order, preventing breaches of the peace, and preventing Election Code violations while the EVBB is 
convened, possessing the same authority as a district judge to perform these duties. If a poll watcher is 
disruptive, impedes the ability of personnel performing their duties, or willfully violates the Election Code, 
the presiding judge may remove the watcher from the EVBB. 
 
[Secs. 32.075, 127.005] 
 
OBSERVING THE EVBB 
If the location cannot accommodate all poll watchers desiring access, the SOS recommends that the EVBB 
manager establish a rotation system. This system should ensure that watchers of opposing interests can 
serve simultaneously and that all watchers receive equal time to observe the activities in that room. 
 
If a poll watcher who was appointed to serve at a polling place will be also serving as a poll watcher at the 
EVBB or CCS, the watcher will need to present a new Certificate of Appointment of Poll Watcher (Form 4-
26, 4-27, 4-28, or 4-29) and Certificate of Completion of Poll Watcher Training administered by the SOS to 
the respective presiding judge.  
  
76 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Appendix A 
 
ACRONYMS AND GLOSSARY 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

 
77 
Alternate Judge: An individual appointed to serve in the capacity of the presiding judge if they are unable 
to perform their duties. 
Canvassing Authority: The governing body responsible for the local canvass of election results. They may 
not canvass until the EVBB finishes processing provisional, late-arriving, and corrective action ballots. 
Carrier Envelope: The envelope used by a voter to return a mail-in ballot, which must be qualified by the 
EVBB before the ballot is counted. 
Central Counting Station (CCS): The central location established for the automatic tabulation of ballots. 
Once the EVBB qualifies and prepares the ballots, they are delivered to the CCS for final counting. 
Clerks: Personnel appointed by the presiding judge to assist in the performance of election duties. 
Corrective Action Process: The procedure that allows a voter to resolve certain defects on their carrier 
envelope to prevent the rejection of their ballot. 
Early Voting Ballot Board (EVBB): Required in every election to process early voting results and review 
provisional ballots. 
Early Voting Clerk: The official responsible for the conduct of early voting and the initial custodian of early 
voting records and ballots . While not a member of the EVBB, the early voting clerk is responsible for 
delivering the jacket envelopes containing mail-in ballots to the EVBB for qualification. The clerk must also 
provide the EVBB with all available information necessary to fulfill its functions, including voter 
registration data. In many entities, the early voting clerk serves as the primary authority for coordinating 
the EVBB convening dates and establishing timelines for the corrective action process. 
General Custodian of Election Records: The official responsible for the secure maintenance of all election 
records, including ballots, electronic media, and video surveillance recordings. Following the conclusion 
of EVBB activities, the general custodian of election records must preserve all records and recordings for 
the duration of the 22-month preservation period for that election. 
Jacket Envelope: The folder or envelope containing the voter’s application for a ballot by mail, the carrier 
envelope, and any accompanying papers for review by the EVBB. 
Late-Arriving Mail Ballots: Ballots received after election day that the EVBB must reconvene to process. 
Limited Ballot: A ballot cast during early voting by a person who is registered in another Texas county but 
has moved to the current county. It contains only the offices and propositions common to both counties 
and must be processed and qualified by the EVBB. 
Livestream Requirement: The statutory mandate for counties with a population of 100,000 or more to 
provide a continuous, publicly accessible video feed of all areas where voted ballots are qualified, 
processed, or stored. 
  
  
78 
Poll Watcher: A person appointed to observe the conduct of an election on behalf of a candidate, political 
party, or the proponents or opponents of a measure. Upon arrival, the watcher must present a  valid 
Certificate of Appointment of Poll Watcher (Form 4-26, 4-27, 4-28, or 4-29) and Certificate of Completion 
of Poll Watcher Training administered by the SOS 
Preservation Period: The 22-month timeframe election records must be maintained. 
Presiding Judge: The official responsible for the overall operation of the EVBB, maintaining order, and 
ensuring all procedures comply with the Election Code. The presiding judge swears in EVBB members, 
issues identification, and makes the final determination on the acceptance or rejection of a ballot if a 
majority of EVBB cannot reach a decision. 
Provisional Ballot: A ballot cast by a voter whose eligibility is in question. These are reviewed by the voter 
registrar and the EVBB before being sent to the CCS for final counting. 
Reconciliation: The process of comparing the number of ballots received, accepted, and rejected against 
the voter list to ensure every ballot is accounted for before records are sent to the CCS. 
Secrecy Envelope:  An internal envelope used to protect b allot privacy within the carrier envelope. If 
missing, the ballot remains valid but must be processed face down. 
Signature Verification Committee (SVC): A committee that may be appointed to perform the initial 
comparison of signatures on mail ballot materials before they are delivered to the EVBB. 
  
 
79 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Appendix B 
 
COMMON SITUATIONS THAT ARISE IN EVBB 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

  
80 
SITUATION 1: TWO BALLOTS OR CARRIER ENVELOPES IN ONE MAILING ENVELOPE 
If you receive an envelope with two carrier envelopes from individuals registered at the same address 
inside and the carrier envelopes are separated (meaning two different carrier envelopes with two 
different ballots), then you may accept the ballots pending any other qualifications.  
 
If you receive an envelope from individuals registered at the same address and the ballots are not 
separated into individual corresponding carrier envelopes (meaning two or more ballots are in one 
carrier), then you may not accept either ballot and both ballots would be rejected. This scenario is often 
found when a couple mails both their ballots in the same carrier envelope. 
 
SITUATION 2: CARRIER ENVELOPE IS EMPTY 
If a carrier envelope appears to be empty, the EVBB should still proceed to check the signature and voter’s 
information on the outside. If the carrier envelope is qualified but the EVBB finds it is empty after opening 
it, the presiding judge must mark “ No Ballot Enclosed” as the reason for rejectio n on the Notice of 
Rejected Ballot (Form 10-22). This ballot should be included in the “ Number of mail ballots rejected by 
board” on the Ballot Transmittal Form for Early Voted Ballots  (Form 10 -6). P lace the empty carrier 
envelope in the envelope that contains the other rejected ballots (which will still be in their carrier 
envelopes). 
 
SITUATION 3: CARRIER ENVELOPE WITNESS PORTION FILLED OUT INCORRECTLY 
If you receive a carrier en velope with the witness portion filled out incorrectly, this is a defect that is 
eligible for correction when identified by the EVBB. Incomplete information about an assistant cannot be 
corrected when identified by the EVBB  and will result in a rejected mail ballot. However, incomplete 
information about an assistant may be corrected when identified by the early voting clerk. 
 
No later than the second day after the EVBB discovers a defect in a carrier envelope and before the EVBB 
decides whether to accept or reject a timely delivered ballot under Section 87.041, the EVBB must send 
the voter a notice of the defect and a corrective action form developed by the SOS by mail or by common 
or contract carrier. Examples of common or contract carriers include UPS, FedEx, DHL, or a local courier 
service.  
 
The EVBB must include with the notice delivered to the voter a brief explanation of each defect in the 
carrier envelope. The notice must also inform the voter that the voter may:  
1. Cancel the voter’s application to vote by mail in the manner described by Section 84.032; or  
2. Correct the defect in the voter’s ballot by:  
a. Submitting a corrective action form developed and made available by the SOS by mail or 
by common or contract carrier; or  
b. Coming to the early voting clerk’s office no later than the sixth day after election day. 
 
  
 
81 
If the EVBB determines that it would not be possible for the voter to receive the notice of defect within a 
reasonable time to correct the defect, the EVBB may notify the voter of the defect by telephone or email 
and inform the voter that the voter may request to have the voter’s application to vote by mail canceled 
in the manner described by Section 84.032, submit a corrective action form developed by the SOS by mail 
or by common or contract carrier, or come to the early voting clerk’s office in person no later than the 
sixth day after election day to correct the defect.  
 
In addition to sending the voter a notice of the defect or notifying the voter of the defect by phone or 
email, the EVBB must permit the voter to correct a defect using the Secretary of State’s Ballot by Mail 
Tracker, if possible. The EVBB no longer has authority under Section 87.0411 to return the defective carrier 
envelope to the voter.  
 
SITUATION 4: WRONG BALLOT IN WRONG CARRIER ENVELOPE DELIVERED TO EVBB 
These scenarios are for a Primary  Runoff/May Uniform Date Election where the county has contracted 
with local entities to serve as the local entities’ early voting clerk.  
 
SCENARIO 1 
The EVBB for the May uniform election is meeting to count ballots. They open a ballot secrecy envelope 
and there is a primary runoff ballot inside. As the ballot secrecy envelope would have been separated from 
the carrier envelope, there would be no way to determine which voter’s ballot this is. 
 
Procedure: This ballot cannot be counted nor retained in a carrier envelope to be forwarded to the EVBB 
for the primary runoff election. The SOS recommends that the EVBB presiding judge make a notation on 
the ballot to explain the situation and why the ballot was not counted. The ballot should be stored in the 
envelope that contains the other rejected ballots (which will still be in their carrier envelopes).  
 
As there is no way to know which voter submitted this ballot, no notice of rejection can be sent to the 
voter. There is no authority in the Texas Election Code to store a voted ballot outside of the jacket or 
carrier envelope. Additionally, while the EVBB qualified the voter’s ballot with respect to the May uniform 
election, the EVBB did not qualify the ballot with respect to the primary runoff. The May uniform EVBB 
does not have the authority to qualify a ballot for the primary runoff. 
 
[Sec. 87.043] 
 
SCENARIO 2A 
The EVBB for the May uniform election reviews a carrier envelope (that is marked to show it is a carrier for 
the May uniform election) and determines it will accept the ballot. The EVBB proceeds to open the carrier 
envelope to remove the ballot secrecy envelope, but the ballot is not in a secrecy envelope. The EVBB is 
able to immediately determine that the ballot inside the carrier is a primary runoff ballot. In this scenario, 
the ballot is tied to a particular voter as the carrier envelope is still effectively with the ballot. 
 
  
  
82 
Procedure: The SOS recommends that the EVBB immediately put the ballot back in the carrier envelope 
and seal the envelope. The EVBB should deliver the carrier envelope to the early voting clerk, who should 
then place the carrier envelope in the jacket envelope for that voter for the primary runoff, ready to be 
forwarded to the EVBB for that election at the appropriate time.  
 
The SOS also suggests that the EVBB presiding judge write a memo to detail what occurred, what actions 
were taken, and the date those actions were taken. The presiding judge and at least one other member 
of the EVBB should sign off on the memo. A copy of the memo should be placed in the voter’s May uniform 
jacket envelope and a copy provided to the early voting clerk for placement in the voter’s primary runoff 
jacket envelope. When the EVBB for the primary runoff election convenes and sees a carrier envelope for 
the May uniform election in the jacket envelope for the primary runoff, the memo will serve to inform 
that EVBB of what has occurred. 
 
SCENARIO 2B 
As a corollary to scenario 2a, as the voter ’s May uniform carrier envelope contained the primary runoff 
ballot, it is possible that the primary runoff carrier contains the May uniform ballot. Can the early voting 
clerk take the primary runoff carrier and provide it to the May uniform election EVBB for processing? 
 
Procedure: As we can identify the voter under these scenarios, and hopefully contact the voter, the chain 
of custody can be established. Regarding the carrier envelope for the runoff, which presumably contains 
the May uniform ballot, the SOS  suggests that the early v oting clerk call the voter (if possible) to see if 
voter can confirm that the May uniform ballot is probably in the runoff carrier envelope. If the voter 
confirms that he or she believes the ballot in the primary runoff carrier envelope is in fact the May uniform 
ballot (or if the early voting clerk is unable to reach voter), the early voting clerk may forward that carrier 
envelope to the May uniform election EVBB to process as normal, if able to do so in a timely manner.  
 
The SOS does not recommend that the early voting clerk open the carrier envelope, with or without the 
voter’s permission, to determine whether the carrier actually contains the May uniform ballot. Only the 
EVBB should be opening this carrier envelope, once the EVBB has determined that th e carrier envelope 
was properly processed (signature comparison completed, voter eligibility determined, etc.).  
 
The SOS suggests that the early voting clerk write a memo to detail what occurred, what actions were 
taken, and the date those actions were taken, and place a copy of the memo in the voter ’s May uniform 
jacket envelope. Another copy should be placed in the voter’s primary runoff jacket envelope. 
 
SCENARIO 3A 
The EVBB for the May uniform election qualifies the carrier envelope and finds two ballots, each inside a 
separate ballot secrecy envelope or neither ballot in a ballot secrecy envelope. 
 
  
 
83 
Procedure: Under this limited circumstance, the EVBB may open the ballot secrecy envelopes, if used by 
the voter. The EVBB has the discretion to open a b allot secrecy envelope in limited circumstances, such 
as to see if there is the Statement of Residence included in the secrecy envelope rather than the carrier 
envelope. It is also not a requirement for a ballot to be in the secrecy envelope. If one of the ballots is for 
the May uniform election and one is for the primary runoff election, the May uniform ballot may be 
counted.  
 
The primary runoff ballot cannot be counted. There is no authority for the EVBB to, for example, copy the 
carrier envelope for the May uniform election and place the runoff ballot back in the carrier envelope for 
forwarding to the primary runoff EVBB (as in scenario 2b, above). The SOS  suggests that the EVBB 
presiding judge makes a notation on the primary runoff ballot to explain the situation and why the ballot 
was not counted. The primary runoff ballot should be stored in the envelope that contains the rejected 
ballots (which will still be in their carrier envelopes).  
 
The SOS also recommends sending this voter a rejection letter, even though this EVBB is not the proper 
board for the primary runoff ballot. As above, it is recommended  that a memo be written and signed by 
the EVBB presiding judge to detail actions taken. A copy of the memo should be placed in the voter’s May 
uniform jacket envelope and a copy provided to the early voting clerk for placement in the voter’s primary 
runoff jacket envelope. 
 
[Sec. 87.043] 
 
SCENARIO 3B 
The EVBB for the May uniform election qualifies the carrier envelope, later discovers that the ballot secrecy 
envelope contains both a May uniform ballot and a primary runoff ballot. 
 
Procedure: As in scenario 3a, the May uniform ballot may be counted, but the primary runoff ballot cannot 
be counted. No notice can be sent to the voter as the identity of the voter cannot be determined by the 
time the error (two ballots in one secrecy envelope) is discovered. Again, the SOS suggests that the EVBB 
presiding judge make a notation on the rejected primary runoff ballot and store it with the rejected May 
uniform ballots. 
 
SITUATION 5: VOTER’S MAILING ADDRESS ON ABBM IS  
DIFFERENT THAN VOTER REGISTRATION ADDRESS ON FILE 
If the grounds for voting by mail is either being 65 or over or disability, and the applicant has not provided 
his or her official mailing address as shown on the list of registered voters as the address for mailing his 
or her ballot, the address provided must be that of a hospital, nursing home, other long term care facility, 
retirement center, or the address of a relative within the second degree by affinity or third degree by 
consanguinity with whom the applicant is living.  If this information was not provided on the ABBM , the 
ballot should be rejected per Section 87.041.

INTRODUCTION 
The Elections Divisio n of the Office of the Secretary of State has prepared this central counting station 
(CCS) handbook. It outlines the roles and responsibilities of CCS personnel and the statutory requirements 
for the tabulating of ballots . It is designed to assist election officials in maintaining an  efficient counting 
process from the time ballots are received until the final unofficial results are released.  Additionally, this 
handbook provides the necessary protocols for maintaining a secure chain of custody and ensuring the 
technical integrity of the electronic voting system. 
 
References are to the appropriate sections in the Texas Election Code, unless otherwise indicated.  
 
The Elections Division of the Office of the Secretary of State is open when the polls are open for voting on 
all uniform election dates.  Answers to questions on election law and procedures  may be obtained by 
calling the Elections Division toll-free at 800-252-VOTE or 512-463-5650. 
 
Visit sos.texas.gov and votetexas.gov for additional election information.  
 
The Office of the Secretary of State does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national orig in, sex, 
religion, age, or disability in employment or the provision of services. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Chapter 1 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
ESTABLISHING A CCS 
 
C C S 
 
2 
Under the Election Code, entities using electronic voting systems can set up a Central Counting Station 
(CCS) to tabulate ballots. This section guides you through the setup process and explains when a CCS is 
required based on your specific voting system configuration. 
 
WHAT IS A CCS? 
A CCS  is a centralized location where ballots cast during an election are counted, vote totals are 
accumulated, and precinct returns are finalized to generate unofficial election results on election night. 
Entities may establish more tha n one CCS for an election. These additional sites, often called regional 
substations or tabulation centers, must adhere to the same statutory requirements as a main CCS. The 
following illustration highlights the ballot processing lifecycle: 
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
IS A CCS NEEDED? 
Whether an entity needs a CCS depends on the type of voting system equipment they use, the way they 
count their ballots, and the way they generate the results for their election. 
 
  

 
3 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
YOU NEED  
A CCS IF: 
You count your ballots by reading 
media from tabulation devices into a 
central computer. 
 
You bring ballots from various 
locations to a central location to be 
scanned.
  
 
You use a central accumulator or 
central scanner to generate 
unofficial results. 
 
 
YOU DO NOT  
NEED A CCS IF: 
Your ballots are hand-counted at the 
precinct polling places on election 
night. 
 
You print tapes at  the precinct and 
generate results by adding totals by 
hand or with a calculator.
  
 
You do not use a central accumulator 
or central scanner. 
 
Whether your entity must establish a CCS depends entirely on your counting method. 
• Electronic Tabulation—If media from tabulation devices is plugged into a central computer  to 
generate results, a CCS must be established.  
• Hand-Counting—This process is strictly decentralized. Ballots may not be brought back to a single 
central location for hand-counting on election night. Instead, poll workers must count election 
day ballots at precinct polling places , w hile the early voting ballot board  (EVBB) handles early 
voting ballots separately. 
 
WHO ESTABLISHES A CCS? 
The CCS is established by the authority that adopts the electronic voting system. This authority varies 
depending on the entity and the type of election. The chart below explains which authority is responsible 
for establishing a CCS for each type of election.

4 
CCS LOCATION 
The CCS must be located in the county in which the political subdivision served by the authority adopting 
the voting system is wholly or partly situated, or in a county contiguous to that county. The CCS should be 
in a location  that can accommodate the needs of t he CCS with respect to space, storage, security, and 
access to applicable voting system equipment or software. 
 
If the CCS is located in an election office or near other election activities, the CCS manager may define 
specific boundaries for the station. This can be done by roping off or clearly marking the perimeter to 
separate non -CCS areas from the CCS. Once marked, all CCS activities must occur strictly within that 
designated area. 
 
[Sec. 127.001]

Chapter 2

The Election Code requires key personnel to be appointed and present whenever the CCS convenes , 
though additional personnel may be appointed to assist as needed. This section outlines the specific roles

Mandatory Appointments 
Each CCS must appoint mandatory personnel, who must be present whenever the CCS convenes. Each 
CCS role must be filled by a separate individual; one person may not serve in multiple roles simultaneously. 
 
CCS Manager 
The CCS manager is in charge of the overall CCS administration and development of the written plan. Both 
the manager and presiding judge may appoint clerks to assist with operations. The manager is entitled to 
compensation in an amount fixed by the authority establishing the CCS.  To be eligible for appointment, 
the manager must have expertise in the specific electronic voting system used.  
 
The general custodian of election records is eligible for this role regardless of whether he or she is a 
candidate or officeholder. Additionally, political subdivision employees may serve as manager and receive 
additional compensation in an amount fixed by the establishing authority. 
 
      
 
      
            
   
   
          
 
 
7 
CCS Presiding Judge 
The presiding judge is responsible for maintaining order, administering oaths, and determining voter 
intent. The presiding judge is appointed in the same way as an election-day presiding judge under Section 
32.002. The judge also confers with and advises the manager and tabulation supervisor on the operation 
of the CCS. 
 
If the manager determines that ballots will be duplicated or manually counted, the clerks will duplicate or 
hand count the ballots, but the presiding judge will resolve any questions concerning voter intent. If the 
presiding judge is absent, the alternate judge serves in the capacity of presiding judge; otherwise, the 
alternate judge performs the duties assigned by the presiding judge. If personnel are granted temporary 
absence from the CCS while the polls are open and the counting of ballots has begun, the presiding judge 
must supervise those absences.  
 
After the tabulation supervisor has prepared the unofficial results (canvassing report), the presiding judge 
must certify their accuracy and prepare documents for proper distribution. For regional substations that 
are used for accumulating results, if the results are transmitted through electronic transmission to the 
CCS, the presiding judge  is responsible for comparing the results transmitted with the results printed at 
the precinct and delivered to the CCS. The presiding judge must also deliver counted ballots and other 
election materials to the custodian of election records.  
 
The presiding judge is also responsible for completing and attesting to the reconciliation forms at the close 
of tabulation on election night and again after the CCS meets for the last time to process provisional, 
corrective action, and late-arriving mail ballots.  
 
A presiding judge is entitled to the same rate as a precinct election judge, except that a judge who serves 
for the entire time at CCS is in operation is entitled to a minimum compensation of five hours’ pay 
regardless of the amount of time worked. 
 
CCS Alternate Judge  
The alternate judge is appointed in the same way as an election day alternate judge under Section 32.002. 
In elections held by a county authority, including the general election for state and county officers , an 
alternate judge must be appointed.  
 
There is no requirement to appoint an  alternate judge for other elections, but the appointing authority 
may appoint one if it chooses to. The alternate judge’s role is to assume the role of the presiding judge if 
the presiding judge is unable to serve.  If the presiding judge is able to serve, then the alternate judge 
performs other duties at the CCS. 
 
An alternate judge is entitled to the same rate as a precinct election judge, except that a judge who serves 
the entire time at CCS is in operation is entitled to a minimum compensation of five hours’ pay regardless 
of the amount of time worked. 
 
 
8 
Co-Judges 
In primary elections,  the appointing authority may appoint two judges. In a separate primary election, 
these judges are the presiding judges of their party’s primary. In a joint primary, they are appointed as co-
presiding judges. In either scenario, both individuals have the authority of a presiding judge. 
 
Each presiding judge will be responsible for resolving voter intent issues and signing precinct returns for 
their own party. Both judges will be responsible for maintaining order in the CCS. In the event of a conflict 
between the presiding judges, the CCS manager is responsible for resolving these conflicts, as the manager 
is in charge of the overall administration of the CCS and the general supervision of the personnel working 
at the station.  
 
Presiding judges/co-judges are entitled to the same rate as a precinct election judge, except that a judge 
who serves for the entire time at CCS is in operation is entitled to a minimum compensation of five hours’ 
pay regardless of the amount of time worked. 
 
Tabulation Supervisor 
The tabulation supervisor is responsible for the operation of the automatic tabulating equipment at the 
CCS and the accumulation of vote totals. The tabulation supervisor is responsible for the security of the 
program and ensures that no person, other than the tabulation supervisor and assistant tabulation 
supervisor(s), operate the tabulation equipment. If the tabulation supervisor is not the programmer, the 
tabulation supervisor must approve the program used to count the ballots before election day. The 
tabulation supervisor is also responsible for the counting of ballots and preparing the unofficial results, 
precinct-by-precinct results, and the overvote and undervote reports. Even though the tabulation 
supervisor prepares these reports, the presiding judge is required to sign them. 
 
To be eligible for appointment, the tabulation supervisor must be trained in the operation of the 
automatic tabulating equipment installed at the CCS. P olitical subdivision employe es may serve as 
tabulation supervisor. The tabulation supervisor is entitled to compensation in an amount fixed by the 
authority establishing the CCS. 
 
 
Optional Appointments 
The Election Code authorizes the appointment of  optional personnel to assist with CCS activities. Unlike 
mandatory roles, these positions are not required to be established for a CCS, and these personnel are 
not required to be present every time the CCS convenes. There is no statutory limit on these 
appointments; however, the appointing authorities should coordinate with the CCS  manager and 
presiding judge to staff the CCS effectively within the operating budget. 
 
Assistant Tabulation Supervisor(s) 
One or more assistants may be appointed by the tabulation supervisor to assist the tabulation supervisor 
in the operation of the tabulating equipment and any other duties as directed by the tabulation 
supervisor. Those appointments must be approved the authority establishing the CCS.   
 
9 
CCS Clerks 
The CCS manager, presiding judge, and alternate judge may each appoint clerks for the CCS. The clerk will 
perform duties that are assigned by the authority that appointed the clerk . A clerk is entitled to 
compensation at the same rate as a precinct election clerk, except that a clerk who serve s for the entire 
time a CCS  is in operation is entitled to a minimum compensation of three hours’ pay regardless of the 
amount of time worked.  
 
[Secs. 127.002, 127.003, 127.004, 127.005, 127.006, 127.123, 127.127, 127.1301, 127.131, 172.126; 1 
TAC 81.148] 
 
APPOINTMENT PROCEDURES FOR CCS PERSONNEL  
The authority establishing the CCS  is responsible for appointing the CCS manager, the tabulation 
supervisor, and the presiding judge and alternate judge. For certain elections, the presiding judge and 
alternate judge are appointed through the list procedure outlined in Section 32.002. Although an assistant 
tabulation supervisor(s) is appointed by the tabulation supervisor, their appointment must be approved 
by the authority establishing the CCS.  
 
If a political subdivision is conducting a joint election with the county or contracting with the county for 
election services, then the political subdivision may delegate the selection of the required personnel to 
the county.  However, the political subdivision is still required to formally appoint the CCS manager , 
tabulation supervisor, presiding judge, and alternate judge as its CCS personnel. The political subdivision’s 
governing body must formally adopt a resolution, order , or take some other formal action appointing 
those individuals as their CCS personnel.

AUTHORIZED PERSONS IN THE CCS 
Section 127.008 provides a list of individuals who may be present in the CCS . No unauthorized persons 
may be present in the CCS. The following individuals are permitted to be present in the CCS:  
• Mandatory and Optional Appointments —CCS manager, tabulation supervisor , assistant 
tabulation supervisor(s), presiding judge, alternate judge, or clerk. 
• Poll Watchers—A poll watcher may serve at a CCS at any time the station is open for the purpose 
of processing or prepa ring to process elections results and until the election officers complete 
their duties at the station. See Poll Watchers for more information. 
• State Inspectors—State inspectors are permitted to be present at and observe any  function or 
activity at the CCS.  
• Voting System Technician—A voting system technician may be present at a CCS  for the purpose 
of repairing, assembling, maintaining, or operating voting system equipment.  
• County Election Officer —As necessary to perform tasks related to the administration of the 
election. 
• Other Individuals Authorized by the Election Code: If authorized under another section of the 
Election Code and with CCS manager approval, the following are included: 
o County Chair in Primary Election:  In a primary election, the county chair is permitted to 
be present in order to supervise the conduct of the primary election and observe the 
tabulation of results. It is a Class B misdemeanor for a county election officer to prevent 
a county chair from performing these duties.  
o Local General Custodian of Election Records: If a local entity is contracting with a county 
for election services, the entity’s general custodian of election records may be present 
under the terms of the election services contract. 
 
[Secs. 31.093(d), 33.055, 34.002, 34.004, 125.010] 
 
REQUIRED OATHS 
Upon convening of the CCS, certain oaths must be administered to personnel: 
• Presiding and Alternate Judges— Before performing any duties, judges must sign the Statement 
of Officer (Form 23-3) and take both the Constitutional Oath of Office  (Form 23-2) and the Oath 
for Central Counting Station Personnel (Form 10-1). 
• All CCS Personnel—The Oath for Central Count ing Station Personnel  (Form 10-1) must be 
administered verbally to all personnel. It is recommended that personnel sign a written copy of 
the oath to maintain a formal record that the oath was properly administered. The oath may be 
administered by anyone authorized to administer oaths under Section 1.016. The following 
statutory language must be used for joint primary elections, the general election for state and 
county offices, and special elections ordered by the governor: 
 
“I swear (or affirm) that I will objectively work to be sure every eligible voter’s vote 
is accepted and counted, and that only the ballots of those voters who violated 
the Texas Election Code will be rejected. I will make every effort to correctly reflect 
the voter’s intent when it can  be clearly determined. I will not work alone when 
ballots are present and will work only in the presence of a member of a political 
 
12 
party different from my own. I will faithfully perform my duty as an officer of the 
election and guard the purity of the election.” 
 
The SOS has prescribed an alternate version of the oath for elections in which party -affiliated 
candidates are not on the ballot or for primary elections that are not conducted jointly: 
 
“I swear (or affirm) that I will objectively work to be sure every eligible voter’s vote 
is accepted and counted, and that only the ballots of those voters who violated 
the Texas Election Code will be rejected. I will make every effort to correctly reflect 
the voter’s intent when it can be clearly determined. I wi ll not work alone when 
ballots are present. I will faithfully perform my duty as an officer of the election 
and guard the purity of the election.” 
 
Members of the CCS are not required to take the election worker oath for polling place workers 
under Section 62.003. 
 
[Secs. 87.006, 127.0015; Tex. Const. Art. XVI, Sec. 1]

Chapter 3 
 
CONVENINING THE CCS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

 
18 
The Election Code outlines specific requirements for when the CCS  may convene and the steps that are 
required to do so. This section address es the timeframes for when the CCS  m ay convene, the 
requirements for convening the CCS , the applicable notice procedures, and the specific procedures 
applicable to counties that convene their CCS before election day as authorized by Section 87.0241(b)(2). 
 
TIME FOR CONVENING THE CCS 
Under Section 87.0241, the CCS  can convene to begin counting early voting ballots at one of two times, 
depending on the size of the county and whether an entity is holding a joint election with the county: 
• When the Polls Open on Election Day—For counties with a population less than 100,000, or local 
entities conducting an election on their own 
• At the End of Early Voting by Personal Appearance—For elections conducted by a county with a 
population of 100,000 or more, or local subdivisions conducting a joint election or conducting an 
election through a contract for election services with a county of 100,000 or more 
 
Regardless of when the CCS  convenes to count the ballots, the election results cannot be released until 
the polls close on election day.  
 
CCS PERSONNEL THAT MUST BE PRESENT TO CONVENE 
The Election Code outlines certain mandatory appointment positions that must be filled for the CCS . In 
order for the CCS to convene, those individuals serving in the mandatory appointment positions must be 
present. The individuals serving in the optional appointment positions are not required to be present for 
the CCS may convene. 
• Mandatory Appointments—CCS manager, tabulation supervisor, presiding judge, and alternate 
judge (for county elections) 
• Optional Appointments—Assistant tabulation supervisor(s) and clerks 
 
NOTICE REQUIREMENTS 
The Election Code and the Texas Administrative Code require notice when the CCS will be convening. The 
law requires that specific forms of notice be delivered to the EVBB presiding judge and that specific notices 
be posted. The requirements vary depending on whether the CCS is convening before, on, or after election 
day: 
 
CCS CONVENES BEFORE ELECTION DAY 
Notice to EVBB: The CCS manager must notify the EVBB presiding judge, in writing, if the CCS will 
convene early. The notice must include the date and time that the presiding judge must deliver ballots 
to the CCS. The notice must be given at least 8 days before the CCS will convene. 
Posting Notice: The CCS manager must post notice of the time and place that the CCS personnel will 
meet. The notice must be posted on the bulletin board used for posting open meetings . The SOS also 
recommends that the notice be posted on the entity’s website. The notice must be posted no later 
than the last day for early voting in person. In the general election for state and county officers, the 
notice must also be sent to each county chair that has a nominee on the general election ballot. 
 
 
19 
CCS CONVENES ON ELECTION DAY 
Notice to EVBB: There is no specific statutory requirement for the CCS manager to provide notice to 
the EVBB presiding judge of when the CCS is convening on election day. The SOS recommends that the 
CCS manager inform the EVBB presiding judge of the time and place that the CCS will convene  on 
election day in case the EVBB needs to make any additional deliveries of processed and accepted ballots 
directly to the CCS. 
Posting Notice: There is no specific statutory requirement for posting notice of when the CCS convenes 
on election day. However, the SOS recommends that the CCS manager post a public notice indicating 
both the time and place that the CCS will convene. The notice should be placed on the bulletin board 
used for pos ting election notices and on the entity’s website, if the entity maintains a website. This 
ensures that all CCS personnel are aware of when they need to be present, and it ensures that poll 
watchers know when they should arrive to observe CCS activities. 
CCS CONVENES AFTER ELECTION DAY 
Notice to EVBB: The CCS manager must notify the EVBB presiding judge whether the CCS will reconvene 
and the date and time that the CCS will reconvene.  
Posting Notice: The CCS manager must post notice at least 24 hours before reconvening the CCS. This 
notice requirement does not roll forward to the next business day if it falls on a weekend or holiday. 
 
To ensure all personnel and poll watchers are informed of when the CCS convenes, the CCS manager may 
utilize the Notice of Convening of Central Counting Station (Form 10-55). 
 
[Secs. 33.055, 87.0241, 127.093, 127.096; 1 TAC 81.36, 1 TAC 81.37, 1 TAC 81.52] 
 
CONVENING CCS BEFORE ELECTION DAY  
Counties with a population of 100,000 or more, or entities conducting their elections jointly or through 
an election-services contract with such a county, are authorized to begin counting early voting ball ots 
after the end of the period for early voting by personal appearance. The Election Code and Administrative 
Code prescribe specific procedural requirements for CCS  activities during this early counting timeframe . 
The CCS manager will determine whether to count the early voted ballots before election day. Any ballots 
received after the EVBB presiding judge delivers ballots to the CCS manager must be counted on election 
day.  
 
Early Convening Procedures 
Procedures may vary slightly based on the type of voting system equipment used and the type of election 
being conducted.  
 
STEP 1 Before counting ballots, zero out any votes on the tabulation device and conduct the Second 
Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment. See Second Test for guidance. 
STEP 2 
Once counting concludes, the  tabulation supervisor must s ecure and s tore the tabulated 
vote data on the appropriate electronic device (such as a removable media device or the  
tabulation computer).  
• Do not print a report showing early voting totals by contest before election day. 
 
20 
STEP 3 
Run a report showing the number of ballots counted for each precinct or polling place. 
Compare these numbers against the Ballot Transmittal Form for Early Voted Ballots  (Form 
10-6) to verify the total ballot count.  
STEP 4 
After the tabulation supervisor has secured and stored the tabulated vote data, zero out the 
tabulation device to conduct the Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment . If this test 
fails, the entire count is void. See Third Test for guidance. 
STEP 5 
On election day (if early voting ballots were counted early) , reload the early voting results 
media into the tabulation software or upload them to the voting system totals. Then, run a 
report of the total ballots counted and compare it directly to the verification report 
generated in Step 3. 
STEP 6 If the two reports show any discrepancy, the early count is void, and all affected ballots must 
be recounted. 
 
[1 TAC 81.36] 
 
LATE CONVENING OF CCS 
There are various deadlines that may impact the date on which the CCS reconvenes to process provisional, 
corrective-action, and late-arriving mail ballots before the final results of the election are canvassed: 
 
 
 
  
• Ballots from voters in the U.S. who submitted an ABBM. 
• Must be postmarked by 7 p.m. on election day and received by early 
voting clerk by 5 p.m. on first business day after election day.

non-military overseas voters who submitted an FPCA. 
• Must be received by early voting clerk no later than  five days after 
election day. 
• Ballot from voters who submitted an FPCA and indicated that they 
are in the military. 
• Must be received by early voting clerk no later than six days after 
election day. 
• Only applicable if there is a curable defect on the voter ’s carrier 
envelope for a ballot by mail. 
• The voter must correct the defect with early voting clerk no later 
than six days after election day. 
• The voter registrar must complete their review of provisional ballots 
within nine days after election day  (or ten days after election day  
for a general election for state and county officers).  
• Following this review, the EVBB meets to qualify the ballots and 
delivers those accepted to the CCS for tabulation. 

 
21 
To ensure compliance with these statutory deadlines, consider utilizing the CCS Reconvening Worksheet.  
 
The last day that the EVBB may meet to accept or reject provisional, corrective action, and late-arriving 
mail ballots is the 9th day after election day (for most elections) or the 13th day after election day (for the 
general election for state and county officers). If the EVBB or the CCS needs to meet after that date, then 
they will need a court order to do so. 
 
If the EVBB has not yet completed its  review of those categories of ballots, then the last meeting of the 
CCS will need to wait until the EVBB has done so.  However, if the EVBB has completed its review of all 
outstanding ballots before the deadline, t hen the CCS may conduct its last meeting once that review is 
complete and those ballots have been delivered. 
 
When the CCS convenes after election day, the CCS manager should coordinate with the EVBB presiding 
judge to determine when the ballots will be available and the final meeting of the CCS should occur. After 
the CCS completes its final meeting to count these categories of ballots, the presiding judge will need to 
provide and attest to a written reconciliation of votes and voters. The presiding judge will use the Election 
Reconciliation - Official Totals (Form 12-2) to complete this process. See Reconciliation of Vote Totals for 
more information on reconciliation procedures. 
 
[Secs. 65.051(a), 86.007, 87.0271, 87.0411, 87.125, 101.057, 127.131]
