Chapter 4 
 
PRE-ELECTION TESTING PROCEDURES 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

 
25 
The Election Code requires several tests and post-election audits of voting system equipment to verify the 
accuracy of that equipment before, during, and after the election. This section addresses the procedures 
for the tests that occur before and during t he election. At least three tests of the automatic tabulating 
equipment are performed before and during each election:  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Third Test of  
Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment Used at a 
Central Counting 
Station 
First Test of Automatic 
Tabulating Equipment 
Used at a Central 
Counting Station 
(conducted during  
the Public L&A Test) 
 
Second Test of 
Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment Used at a 
Central Counting 
Station 
 
EQUIPMENT THAT MUST BE TESTED 
Each of these three  tests involves the testing of specific voting system equipment that is used in an 
election. The equipment requirements for each test are outlined below. 
 
Equipment for Public L&A Test and First Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment  
The test must include a representative sample of each type of equipment that will be used in the election, 
including any: 
• Ballot marking devices; 
• Direct recording electronic  voting 
machines (DRE); 
• Any other devices used by the voter to 
mark or cast their ballot; 
• Precinct scanners; 
• Central scanners; and 
• Tabulation computers. 
 
A representative sample of each of these devices must be tested during the Public L ogic and Accuracy 
(L&A) Test if those devices will be used in the election. If any centra l scanners or tabulation computers 
will be used in the election, that equipment must be tested during the  First Test of Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment. 
 
Equipment for Second and Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment  
The test will be performed using the media that was generated in the First Test of Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment. The test must be performed using each of the tabulation computers that will be used in the 
election.  
 
26 
PRE-ELECTION TESTING REQUIREMENTS 
The Public L&A Test and First Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment are conducted together by a single 
testing board, take place simultaneously, and are open to the public to determine whether the system is 
accurately marking and tabulating ballots. 
 
The First Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment is designed to test all automatic tabulating equipment, 
whether it is used at a polling place (like precinct scanners) or at a CCS (like central scanners and tabulation 
computers). Precinct scanners are only tested once during the First Test of Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment. Central scanners and tabulation computers are tested during the First, Second, and Third Test 
of Automatic Tabulating Equipment. 
 
The Public L&A Test and First Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment must be conducted at leas t 48 
hours before the equipment is used to count ballots in an election. If this deadline cannot be met, the 
general custodian of election records must conduct the test as soon as practicable after that date. In such 
cases, the SOS must be notified within 24 hours of determining that the deadline cannot be met. 
 
This testing process allows the authority conducting the election to identify any errors in ballot 
programming and address those issues before ballots are sent to voters and before voting system 
equipment is deployed to the polling places used in the election. 
 
[Secs. 127.093, 127.096, 129.023] 
 
PUBLIC L&A TEST AND FIRST TEST OF AUTOMATIC TABULATING 
EQUIPMENT 
Notice Requirements  
The Public Notice of Public Logic and Accuracy Test and First Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment  
(Form 15-6) must be published on the entity’s website at least 48 hours before the test begins. If the entity 
does not maintain a website, then the notice must be posted on the bulletin board used for posting 
meetings of the governing body.  
 
If the
 test is being conducted for a primary election, then the general custodian of election records must 
notify the county chair of the test at least 48 hours before the test begins, and the county chair must 
confirm receipt of the notice. If the test is being conducted for an election for which the county election 
board is established, then the general custodian must notify each member of the county election bo ard 
at least 48 hours before the test begins.  
 
Note: The Public Notice of Public Logic and Accuracy Test and First Test of Automatic Tabulating  
Equipment is no longer required to be published in the newspaper.  
 
[Secs. 127.096, 129.023] 
 
 
27 
Testing Procedures and Requirements 
The general custodian of election records must develop written procedures for the tests. A test script is a 
set of instructions for marking and casting a predetermined number of votes. This creates a “test deck” of 
ballots that is scanned and counted by the voting system so the results can be compared against the 
script’s known outcome. The written testing procedures must include: 
• Verifying that each contest position, precinct, and ballot style on the ballot can be voted and is 
accurately counted; 
• Accounting for overvotes and undervotes for each race; 
• Including write-in votes, when applicable; 
• Processing provisional votes electronically, if applicable to the voting system being used; 
• Ensuring that each type of automatic tabulating equipment, ballot marking device, and DRE device 
used in the election is tested; 
• Incorporating each type of ballot used in the election into the test deck, including mail ballot stock 
and ballots marked by ballot marking devices; 
• Marking and labeling test ballots clearly to ensure they are never accidentally used or mixed into 
an upcoming live election; 
• Verifying that the public counter on all tabulation devices is set to zero before the test begins; 
• Verifying that the public counter on all tabulation devices is set to zero and printing a zero report 
(or zero tape) before the test deck is processed; 
• Testing accessibility features, which requires that at least one vote be cast and verified by a two -
person testing board team using those features; 
• Calculating the expected results from the test script prior to running the deck; 
• Comparing the pre-calculated expected results to the actual tabulated results of the test; and 
• Performing a hash validation on a representative sample of the voting devices used  with the 
system. 
o For the hash validation, a "representative sample" means at least ten of each voting 
device, or 5% of each type of voting device, whichever number is fewer. 
 
 

 
28 
Conducting the Test  
The test must be performed by a testing board consisting of at least two persons. The general custodian  
of election records must make a reasonable effort to ensure that the testing board includes at least one 
person from each political party that holds a primary election.  
 
If the testing board determines that a test was unsuccessful, the general custodian of election records  
must prepare a written explanation identifying the cause of the failure and publish that explanation 
online. The general custodian of election records must retain the materials used in the unsuccessful test. 
After the identified issue is resolved, the general custodian of election records  must conduct another 
public test, repeating the process until a successful test is completed.  
 
Certification and Preservation 
The test is considered successful only when the pre-calculated expected results perfectly match the actual 
tabulated results. After a successful test is completed, the testing board and the general custodian must 
sign a written statement attesting to the qualification of each voting device that was successfully tested, 
documenting any problems discovered, and noting the cause of any identified issues. If a member of the 
county election board chooses to witness the test, they must also sign this statement. The Certification of 
Public Logic and Accuracy Test and First Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment  (Form 15-5) must be 
completed and signed by the testing board and the general custodian. 
 
Once f
inalized, the general custodian will place all test materials (including the electronic media generated 
by the test) into a container and secure it with a seal signed by the custodian and at least two members 
of the testing board. These test materials must remain sealed for the duration of the 22 -month 
preservation period for that election. The container may not be unsealed unless the contents are 
necessary to conduct another test, or are required for a criminal investigation, election contest,  public 
inspection request, or other official proceeding under the Election Code. The test materials are not 
available for public inspection until the first day after the final canvass of the main election is completed. 
 
[Secs. 127.094, 127.095, 127.099, 129.023, 129.024] 
 
SECOND TEST OF AUTOMATIC TABULATING EQUIPMENT 
The Second Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment must be conducted immediately before each time 
the CCS convenes to count ballots. Before performing the test, the CCS manager and the presiding judge 
must verify that the seal on the container holding the test materials from the First Test of Automatic 
Tabulating Equipment is intact. After verification, they will break the seal and remove the materials for 
the tabulation supervisor, who will reuse the test deck to run the test. The test is successful if the results 
perfectly match the First Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment. 
 
The presiding judge must certify the success, date, and hour on the Certification of Second Test of 
Automatic Tabulating Equipment Used at the Central Counting Station (Form 15-1), which is then retained 
with the test materials. Immediately following this certification, the tabulation supervis or must clear the 
equipment's memory to completely erase the test data before official live ballot tabulation begins.  
 
 
29 
Once the memory is cleared, the tabulation supervisor must 
print a zero report (or zero tape) to prove that the device or 
central accumulator contains absolutely no previously 
scanned ballots or residual data. Both the tabulation 
supervisor and the presiding judge must sign and date these 
zero reports to verify the zero balance. 
 
THIRD TEST OF AUTOMATIC TABULATING 
EQUIPMENT 
Immediately af ter a counting session is completed (or each 
time the CCS adjourns), the equipment must be tested one 
final time to ensure it functioned accurately throughout the 
entire live tabulation process. The CCS manager and the 
presiding judge must verify that the temporary seal on the 
container holding the test materials is intact, break the seal, 
and hand the test deck to the tabulation supervisor. 
 
The tabulation supervisor will perform the Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment using the exact 
same test materials. The test is successful if the results perfectly match the First Test  of Automatic 
Tabulating Equipment. The presiding judge must certify the success, date, and hour on the Certification 
of Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment Used at the Central Counting Station (Form 15-3), which 
is retained with the test materials. 
 
HANDLING UNSUCCESSFUL TESTS 
If either of the tests are unsuccessful, the testing authority must document the cause of the discrepancy 
in writing and repeat the test process. If a subsequent retry succeeds, the specific corrective actions taken 
to achieve that result must be fully documented and retained with the test materials.  If a successful test 
cannot be achieved after troubleshooting: 
• Unsuccessful Second Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment—Ballots cannot be processed on 
that machine and must be counted manually, if applicable, or with other tabulating equipment. 
• Unsuccessful Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment—The entire ballot count is void, and 
ballots must be recounted manually, if applicable, or with other tabulating equipment. 
 
SECURING, PRESERVING, AND INSPECTING TEST MATERIALS 
After both the Second Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment and the Third Test of Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment are completed and certified, the presiding judge must secure the test materials in a container 
and seal it. The CCS manager, tabulation supervisor, presiding judge, and up to two watchers of opposing 
interests (if present) must sign the seal. 
 
Note: The seal applied after the Second Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment is temporary to maintain 
the integrity of the test deck  during ballot counting and must be broken to conduct the Third Test of 
Automatic Tabulating Equipment. 
 

 
30 
Following the Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment, the test materials must remain sealed for 
the duration of the 22 -month preservation period for that election. The container may not be unsealed 
unless the contents are necessary to conduct another  test, or if they are needed for a criminal 
investigation, election contest, request for public inspection, or other official proceeding under the 
Election Code. These materials are not available for public inspection until the first day after the final 
canvass of the main election is completed.  
 
[Sec. 127.093, 127.097, 127.098, 127.099]

Chapter 5 
 
TABULATION PROCEDURES AT THE CCS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

 
36 
The CCS is responsible for the counting of ballots and the tabulation of results. As part of this process, the 
CCS must manage several different procedures, including the intake of ballots, electronic media, and other 
supplies; duplication of ballots that cannot be read through the tabulating equipment; testing of 
tabulation systems; loading electronic media and scanning any physical ballots; adjudication of write-in 
votes; resolution of voter-intent issues; and tabulation and reconciliation of votes. This section addresses 
the applicable procedures for those activities at the CCS. 
 
INTAKE OF BALLOTS, ELECTRONIC MEDIA, AND SUPPLIES 
The CCS manager should establish specific procedures for intaking ballots, electronic media, and any 
supplies delivered from polling places. These steps may vary depending on the type of voting system 
equipment used in the election and the manner in which ballots are cast, but they must include methods 
for verifying the chain of custody, resolving chain of custody documentation discrepancies, and managing 
and distributing those records to the CCS areas where those records will be stored or used.  The CCS 
manager may use the following steps as a template for designing their own intake plan:  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
All paperwork—such as serial                      
number logs, chain of custody forms,                  
and ballot and seal certificates—              
must be completed showing that                  
every record is accounted for.  
  
Sort through all ballots and/or electronic              
media containing votes to identify                   
damaged ballots, write-in votes, or other               
issues requiring special handling. Any                
identified items should be separated and 
delivered to the appropriate CCS personnel. 
 
The remaining ballots and/or                       
electronic media must be delivered to             
the tabulation supervisor for counting             
or accumulation of vote totals.  
 
If there is a discrepancy, CCS personnel          
must contact the presiding judge of          
the polling place to determine the            
basis for the discrepancy. 
 
CCS personnel must verify that all                        
locks and seals are properly affixed          
to the equipment and/or secure                  
container for completed envelopes. 
 
CCS personnel must inspect                       
the equipment or secure container               
for completed envelopes to                   
determine if the serial number                    
on the seal corresponds to the serial 
numbers on their records.    
Upon receipt of the election records,                   
ballots, and/or electronic media, the            
presiding judge or the judge’s designees 
must give a signed receipt for materials 
delivered to one of the delivering officers. 
 
Consider utilizing the Procedures for the Intake of Materials Workbook to help develop and document the 
CCS intake strategy. 
 
[Secs. 127.068, 127.069, 129.051]  
      
    
      
                        
                            
                                    
                
 
         
    
      
                      
                     
 
37 
TESTING REQUIREMENTS 
The Second Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment  must be performed immediately before each time 
that the ballots are counted using the tabulating equipment, while the Third Test of Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment must be performed immediately after each time that counting is completed.  See Pre-Election 
Testing Procedures for guidance on the applicable procedures. 
 
[Sec. 127.093] 
 
TABULATION PROCEDURES  
Tabulation procedures will generally vary significantly for each entity depending on the size of the entity, 
the voting system equipment used in the election, and the manner in which the ballots are to be counted 
for that election.  Each voting system has specific steps involved in conducting the procedures outlined 
below. The tabulation supervisor and assistant tabulation supervisor(s) are the only individuals authorized 
to operate the automatic tabulating equipment or handle ballots that are automatically counted. For 
more guidance on the specific process for your voting system, consult with your voting system vendor.  
 
[Sec. 127.127] 
 
Precinct Scanners at the Polling Place  
For entities that count their ballots by having voters deposit their ballots directly into precinct scanners 
at the polling place, the tabulation process will largely consist of reading the electronic media containing 
that voted ballot data into the central tabulation computer at the CCS. 
 
General Procedures 
After the intake process (including chain of custody verifications) has been completed, the tabulation 
supervisor will generally begin the process of reading in the media and tabulating those results on the 
central computer. 
 
As the media is loaded into the central computer, the tabulation supervisor must verify that the vote totals 
on the electronic media match the vote totals on the printed results tape, if applicable. After uploading 
all precinct results to the central computer, the election official must verify and document that the central 
computer’s total number of votes cast in an election matches the number of  signatures on the 
combination form. If there is a discrepancy, the presiding judge, in conjunction with the CCS manager, 
must determine if a further investigation is necessary. 
 
The CCS manager and tabulation supervisor should establish procedures for tra cking the media through 
the process so that they can distinguish which media drives have been read into the system, which drives 
have been received at the CCS but not yet read into the system, and which drives have not yet been 
received at the CCS.  The CCS  manager and tabulation supervisor  should also establish procedures for 
regular verification checks to ensure that the media has been read correctly and that results are being 
tabulated accurately. 
 
Precinct returns will be generated through the voting system. The presiding judge will sign and certify the 
precinct returns.  
 
38 
Ballots Deposited into Emergency Slot at Polling Place 
If a precinct scanner is malfunctioning or the ballot is damaged in a manner that results in the voter being 
unable to deposit the ballot directly into the precinct scanner, then the voter should deposit their ballot 
into the emergency slot on the precinct scanner enclosure. This is a separate compartment on the ballot 
box that allows for the voter to deposit their ballot, while segre gating that ballot from other ballots that 
have already been counted by the precinct scanner. The ballots placed in the emergency slot must not be 
commingled with the ballots that were properly scanned by the precinct scanner and deposited into the 
ballot box. 
 
The ballots in the emergency slot should be delivered to the CCS for counting using the automatic 
tabulating equipment at the location and/or duplication by the CCS m anager in the event that the ballot 
is damaged in a manner that makes it unreadable. These ballots must be scanned at the CCS and may not 
be scanned through the precinct scanner at the polling place.  
 
Ballot and Seal Certificate Procedures 
If the ballot count on the Combined Register of Official Ballots and Ballot and Seal Certificate (Form 7-26)  
differs from the precinct scanner’s results tape by four or more, the ballots must be officially tabulated at 
the CCS. This requirement helps identify possible precinct scanner malfunctions by providing an 
alternative tabulation process. CCS personnel should review the paperwork completed by the presiding 
judge of the election day polling place to determine whether a discrepancy exists that would require the 
ballots to be tabulated at the CCS.  If a discrepancy of four or more is found, the original count of the 
ballots from the precinct scanner is void, and the ballots must be processed using the automatic tabulating 
equipment at the CCS. 
 
[Secs. 125.006, 127.126, 127.131, 127.156] 
 
Ballots Deposited into Ballot Boxes and Centrally Scanned at CCS 
For entities that count their ballots by having voters deposit their ballots into a ballot box at the polling 
place, the tabulation process primarily involves scanning those ballots at the CCS. Following intake, the 
CCS manager must have the ballots prepared for automatic counting. Any irregularly marked ballots must 
be duplicated to reflect the voter’s intent under the procedures outlined in the Duplication section below. 
The presiding judge is responsible for determining the voter’s intent. 
 
Once prepared, ballots are delivered to the tabulation supervisor (or designee), who operates the  
equipment for counting. As ballots are processed, the presiding judge must prepare a report from each 
scanner regarding the total number of ballots scanned  onto each  media drive. This report must be 
generated from the scanner before the media drive is read into a tabulation computer. If prepared before 
the polls are opened on election day (such as in a county over 100,000 that is convening a CCS after the 
end of early voting), the report cannot contain any results information about the total number of vote s 
received for each candidate or for or against each measure. Finally, the presiding judge signs and certifies 
the precinct returns generated by the voting system. 
 
[Secs. 127.005, 127.125, 127.126, 127.127, 127.1302, 127.131] 
 
 
39 
DRE Systems 
For entities that count their ballots by having voters deposit their ballots directly into precinct scanners 
at the polling place, the tabulation process will largely consist of reading the electronic media containing 
that voted ballot data into the central tabulation computer at the CCS. 
 
As the media is loaded into the central computer, the tabulation supervisor must verify that the vote totals 
on the electronic media match the vote totals on the printed results tape, if applicable. After uploading 
all precinct results to the central computer, the election official must verify and document that the central 
computer’s total number of votes cast in an election matches the number of signatures on the 
combination form. If there is a discrepancy, the presiding judge, in conjunction with the CCS manager, 
must determine if a further investigation is necessary. 
 
The CCS manager and tabulation supervisor should establish procedures for tracking the media through 
the process so that they can distinguish which media drives have been read into the system, which drives 
have been received at the CCS but not yet read into the system, and which drives have not yet been 
received at the CCS.  The CCS manager and tabulation supervisor  should also establish procedures for 
regular verification checks to ensure that the media has been read correctly and that results are being 
tabulated accurately. 
 
Precinct returns will be generated through the voting system. The presiding judge will sign and certify the 
precinct returns.  
 
[Sec. 127.131]

Chapter 6 
 
RESOLVING VOTER INTENT 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

 
42 
The presiding judge is responsible for resolving questions of voter intent at the CCS . If a voter’s ballot 
contains ambiguous markings, then the presiding judge will determine the voter’s intent and the ballot 
will be counted according to that intent. The process for determining the voter’s intent and counting the 
ballot according to that intent will depend on the voting system used in the election. This section 
addresses the legal requirements and procedures for voter intent resolution. For more information on the 
specific steps for conducting this process with your voting system, please contact your voting system 
vendor. 
 
PRECINCT SCANNERS AT THE POLLING PLACE 
Ballots Marked by Ballot Marking Devices 
When voters mark their ballots using electronic ballot marking devices, the voter adjudicates their intent 
on the device. Because electronic ballot marking devices alert the voter to undervotes and require the 
voter to adjudicate overvotes before printing their marked ballot, those voter intent issues do not require 
resolution by the presiding judge at the CCS. However, write-in votes require adjudication by the presiding 
judge, even when the voter is using an electronic ballot marking device to mark their ballot.  Those 
procedures are addressed in more detail below.  
 
[Secs. 65.009, 127.005, 127.130] 
 
Hand-Marked Ballots 
When a voter inserts a hand-marked ballot into a precinct scanner, the precinct scanner will identify 
overvotes and undervotes, and provide the voter with an opportunity to resolve those voter intent issues 
before casting their ballot. However, write-in votes require adjudication by the presiding judge. Those 
procedures are addressed in more detail below.  
 
BALLOTS DEPOSITED INTO BALLOT BOXES AND SCANNED AT CCS 
If optical scan ballots are used in a precinct without a precinct scanner, the ballots are deposited by the 
voter in a pre-locked and pre-sealed ballot box. When the ballots arrive at the CCS , the CCS manager will 
have the ballots examined to determine whether there are any irregularly-marked ballots. Any irregularly 
marked ballots should be duplicated to reflect the voter’s intent under the procedures outlined in the 
Duplication section below. 
 
Alternatively, if the automatic counting of thos e irregularly marked ballots is impracticable, the CCS 
manager may direct that the ballots be manually counted. In that situation, the manual count would be 
conducted under the procedures for conducting a hand -count under Chapter 65, which are outlined in 
the Election Judges and Clerks Handbook . The results from the manual count will also be tabulated by 
precinct and will be added to the totals generated from the automatic tabulating equipment before the 
unofficial results are released. 
 
If there is any dispute regarding a voter’s intent, the CCS presiding judge  is the final authority on 
determining intent.  
 
 
43 
DRE Systems 
When voters mark their ballots using DRE dev ices, the voter adjudicates their intent on the device.  
Because DRE devices alert the voter to undervotes and require the voter to adjudicate overvotes before 
printing their marked ballot, those voter intent issues do not require resolution by the presidin g judge at 
the CCS. However, write-in votes require adjudication by the presiding judge, even when the voter is using 
a DRE device to mark their ballot. Those procedures are addressed in more detail below.  
 
[Secs. 127.005, 127.125, 127.126, 127.130, 127.131] 
 
DUPLICATION  
When electronic tabulation systems are used in the conduct of voting, ballots that are unable to be 
scanned by the precinct tabulator or central scanner must be remade using the duplication procedures. 
Several common issues can necessitat e the duplication of ballots to ensure that every vote is counted 
accurately and legally. If there are any ballots that must be duplicated, the CCS manager may have ballots 
duplicated for automatic counting, but must follow specific procedures. The manager may be assisted by 
other CCS personnel in performing this process. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Ballot Unable  
to Be Scanned 
 
 
The ballot must be duplicated to reflect the intent of the voter, and the presiding judge is responsible for 
determining issues of voter intent.  The duplication process can be performed manually using hand -
marked ballots or can be performed using electronic ballot marking devices. When the ballots are 
duplicated, the duplicate ballot must be clearly labeled “Duplicate,” and the serial number of the original 
ballot must be placed on the duplicate ballot.

44 
After the ballot is duplicated and the ballots have been approved for counting by the CCS manager, the 
duplicate ballot will be counted using the automatic tabulating equipment.  The original ballot and the 
duplicate ballot should be retained together, and must  be retained with the other voted ballots for the 
duration of the 22-month preservation period for that election. 
 
 [Secs. 127.005, 127.125, 127.126]  
 
Examples of Ballots That Must Be Duplicated 
Ballot duplication is primarily required for the reasons shown below: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Physical Damage to the Ballot 
 
Damage may occur during normal delivery, voting, processing, or 
scanning. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Unreadable Ballot Marks 
 
Ballots marked with inappropriate tools, such as pencils, 
highlighters, colored pens, chalk, cosmetic pencils, paints, 
crayons, and colored art pencils, cannot be processed by 
standard tabulation systems because scanners cannot read these 
marks. The  law allows for the duplication of ballots marked in 
pencil or an un-scannable pen color. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Improper Ballot Specifications 
 
Ballots printed on poor -quality paper or incorrect sizes can be 
unreadable by scanning equipment. When an overseas voter uses 
a personal printer to print an emailed ballot, A4-sized paper may 
be used instead of the U.S. standard of 8.5 x 11 inches. Ballot size 
differences can affect image quality. This includes Federal Write-
In Absentee Ballots (FWABs). 
 
 
 
45 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Un
 
A voter’s intent or marking may be unclear or may not align with 
tabulation requirements. For example, circling a candidate or 
marking adjacent ovals can lead to overvotes or undervotes. It  is 
essential for a team of two people to agree on the voter’s intent 
when duplicating the ballot. Remember, the presiding judge of 
the central counting station resolves all issues of voter intent. 
clear Voter Markings 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
B
 
allot Misprints 
When a mistake occurs during the printing process, one or more 
ballots may not be able to be scanned by the automatic 
tabulation equipment.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Damaged Timing Marks 
 
Small tears, wrinkles, coffee spills as well as stray marks made by 
the voter can interfere with the scanning process. 
 
ADJUDICATING WRITE-IN VOTES 
Write-in votes that are cast on electronic voting systems generally require adjudication to assign those 
votes to a declared write -in candidate.  The presiding judge is responsible for reviewing those write-in 
votes and determining whether the voter’s write-in selection corresponds to a declared write-in candidate 
in the election. In conducting this adjudication process, the presiding judge should adopt specific 
standards for determining voter intent with regard to write-in selections and must apply those standards 
consistently to all voters and candidates in the election.  
 
If a voter writes in a name not found on the List of Declared Write -In Candidates (Form 3-5), the vote is 
not counted. This applies to the November general election, city council officer elections, independent or 
common school district trustee election s, hospital district elections , special elections for state 
representative and state senator, as well as any other elections requiring a declaration of write-in.

Any write-in votes that were cast on or before election day must be adjudicated no later than election 
night, and must be reported as part of the unofficial results that are reported on election night.  The 
presiding judge may be assisted by their clerks or designees during the adjudication process, provided 
these individuals follow the judge’s established voter intent standards. Additionally, the tabulation 
supervisor, assistant supervisor(s), or other CCS personnel may operate the voting system equipment 
required for this process. The personnel assisting with the adjudication process should be an equal 
number of individuals who are affiliated or aligned with each political party with nominees on the bal lot, 
if applicable.

Chapter 7 
 
COUNTING PROVISIONAL, LATE-ARRIVING,  
AND CORRECTIVE ACTION MAIL BALLOTS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
48 
COUNTING PROVISIONAL BALLOTS  
The CCS will generally need to meet again after election day to count provisional ballots after they have 
been reviewed by the voter registrar and accepted for counting by the EVBB . The Texas Administrative 
Code outlines specific procedures for how the provisional ballots are to be processed and counted at the 
CCS. These procedures are outlined below. 
 
Procedures for Counting Ballots with Paper-Based Systems  
 
STEP 1 
If provisional ballots were cast on a scannable paper ballot, the CCS manager must decide 
whether the EVBB must manually count the ballots and manually add to the computer count 
for a canvass total or whether the CCS must reconvene.  
STEP 2 The manager must notify the EVBB presiding judge as to whether or not the CCS  will 
reconvene to count the ballots. 
STEP 3 If the provisional ballots will be counted at the CCS , then the EVBB presiding judge and the 
manager should coordinate the delivery of those materials to the CCS. 
STEP 4 
When the provisional ballots arrive at the CCS, the presiding judge must inspect the secure 
container for completed envelopes and complete the Verification of Provisional Ballots and 
Serial Numbers (Form 9-7). 
STEP 5 The provisional ballots must be removed from the secure container for completed 
envelopes and given to the manager and tabulation supervisor for counting.  
STEP 6 Prior to the beginning of the count at a CCS , the manager must run the Second Test  of the 
Automatic Tabulation Equipment. The test must be successful. 
STEP 7 
After the successful Second Test of the Automatic Tabulation Equipment  is conducted, the 
unofficial election results, preserved by electronic means, must be loaded in the tabulating 
equipment. 
STEP 8 Once the ballots have been counted, the results must be prepared in the regular manner. 
STEP 9 
The manager must prepare and sign the Certification of Second Test of Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment Used at the Central Counting Station (Form 15-1). This cer tification confirms the 
equipment was functioning properly before the count began. 
STEP 10 Immediately after the results are prep ared, the tabulation supervisor must run the Third 
Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment. This test must be successful to validate the count. 
STEP 11 
Upon the successful completion of the Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment , the 
manager and tabulation supervisor must complete and sign the Certification of Third Test 
of Automatic Tabulating Equipment Used at the Central Counting Station (Form 15-3). 
STEP 12 
Attach both the Second and Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment Certifications to 
the returns. Deliver these records to the presiding officer of the canvassing authority. The 
certifications should indicate that these results supersede any returns printed prior to t he 
reconvening of the CCS. 
STEP 13 
Once the count and testing are finalized, re-seal the Affidavit of Provisional Voter Envelopes 
and corresponding paperwork in the secure container and return it to the general custodian 
of election records. 
 
49 
[1 TAC 81.176(c)(8), 1 TAC 81.176(c)(10)] 
 
Procedures for Counting Ballots Cast on a DRE 
 
STEP 1 If provisional ballots were cast on a DRE, the CCS  must reconvene to count accepted 
provisional ballots. 
STEP 2 The EVBB presiding judge  and the CCS manager should coordinate the delivery of those 
materials to the CCS. 
STEP 3 The accepted provisional ballots must be transported to the CCS  in a secure container for 
completed envelopes. 
STEP 4 
The manager must prepare the DRE voting system for reviewing and ac cepting provisional 
ballots in accordance with instructions provided by the general custodian of election 
records, which may include the instructions of the vendor of the system. 
STEP 5 
When the provisional ballots arrive at the CCS, the presiding judge of the CCS must inspect 
the secure container for completed envelopes and complete the Verification of Provisional 
Ballots and Serial Numbers (Form 9-7).   
STEP 6 The provisional  ballots must be removed from the secure container for completed 
envelopes and given to the manager and tabulation supervisor for counting.  
STEP 7 Prior to the beginning of the count at a CCS, the manager must run the Second Test  of the 
Automatic Tabulation Equipment. The test must be successful. 
STEP 8 
After the successful Second Test  of the Automatic Tabulation Equipment  is conducted, the 
unofficial election results, preserved by electronic means, must be loaded in the tabulating 
equipment. 
STEP 9 Once the ballots have been counted, the results must be prepared in the regular manner. 
STEP 10 
The manager must prepare and sign the Certification of Second Test of Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment Used at the Central Counting Station (Form 15-1). This cer tification confirms the 
equipment was functioning properly before the count began. 
STEP 11 Immediately after the results are prep ared, the tabulation supervisor must run the Third 
Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment. This test must be successful to validate the count. 
STEP 12 
Upon the successful c ompletion of the Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment , the 
manager and tabulation supervisor must complete and sign the Certification of Third Test 
of Automatic Tabulating Equipment Used at the Central Counting Station (Form 15-3). 
STEP 13 
Attach both the Second and Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment Certifications to 
the returns. Deliver these records to the presiding officer of the canvassing authority. The 
certifications should indicate that these results supersede any returns printed prior to the 
reconvening of the CCS. 
STEP 14 
Once the count and testing are finalized, re-seal the Affidavit of Provisional Voter Envelopes 
and corresponding paperwork in the secure container and return it to the general custodian 
of election records. 
 
 [1 TAC 81.176(c)(9), 1 TAC 81.176(c)(10)]  
 
50 
COUNTING LATE-ARRIVING AND CORRECTIVE ACTION MAIL BALLOTS 
The CCS typically reconvenes after election day to count late -arriving mail ballots and ballots that were 
corrected by voters  through the corrective -action process after those ballots have been accepted for 
counting by the EVBB. See Convening the CCS for categories of ballots that are subject to counting under 
these procedures. If these ballots will be counted at the CCS, the EVBB presiding judge and CCS manager 
must coordinate the delivery of those materials. The manager is required to post a noti ce of the CCS 
convening at least 24 hours before the CCS convenes to count those ballots. 
 
STEP 1 The EVBB presiding judge must complete a Ballot Transmittal Form for Early Voted Ballots  
(Form 10-6) that accompanies the qualified ballots to the CCS.  
STEP 2 Prior to the beginning of the count at a CCS, the manager must run the Second Test  of the 
Automatic Tabulation Equipment. The test must be successful. 
STEP 3 
After the successful Second Test of the Automatic Tabulation Equipment  is conducted, the 
unofficial election results, preserved by electronic means, must be loaded in the tabulating 
equipment. 
STEP 4 
The tabulation supervisor must print a report showing what votes have been tabulated or 
accumulated on that equipment before the counting begins. This status report must be 
compared with the report (unofficial election results) run on election night. If the status 
report matches the report run on election night, the tabulation supervisor may order the 
count to begin. If the two reports do not match, the electronic ballots must be counted by 
hand and manually added to the returns printed on election night.  
STEP 5 Once the ballots have been counted, the results must be prepared in the regular manner. 
STEP 6 
The manager must prepare and sign the Certification of Second Test of Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment Used at the Central Counting Station (Form 15-1). This certification confirms the 
equipment was functioning properly before the count began. 
STEP 7 Immediately after the results are prep ared, the tabulation supervisor must run the Third 
Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment. This test must be successful to validate the count. 
STEP 8 
Upon the successful completion of the Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment , the 
manager and tabulation supervisor must complete and sign the Certification of Third Test 
of Automatic Tabulating Equipment Used at the Central Counting Station (Form 15-3). 
STEP 9 
Attach both the Second and Third Test of Automatic Tabulating Equipment Certifications to 
the returns. Deliver these rec ords to the presiding officer of the canvassing authority. The 
certifications should indicate that these results supersede any returns printed prior to the 
reconvening of the CCS. 
STEP 10 
Once the count and testing are finalized, re-seal the Affidavit of Provisional Voter Envelopes 
and corresponding paperwork in the secure container and return it to the general custodian 
of election records. 
 
[1 TAC 81.37]

Chapter 8 
 
PREPARING RETURNS AND DISTRIBUTING ELECTION RECORDS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
53 
When a CCS is established for an election, the precinct returns and election results will be generated at 
the CCS rather than at the precinct polling places on election day. This section addresses the requirements 
relating to the preparation of the election returns,  the rules governing the announcement of unofficial 
results, and the requirements for the distribution of the election records after the CCS  has completed its 
process. 
 
GENERATING ELECTION RESULTS AND PRECINCT RETURNS 
After the counting of ballots (or accu mulation of vote totals) has occurred, the presiding judge  is 
responsible for preparing the precinct election returns. The presiding judge is required to sign the precinct 
returns to certify their accuracy. If you are using a voting system’s certified software to assist you with the 
accumulation and printing of reports, the printed “precinct-by-precinct” report that has been adjusted to 
include any hand -counted ballots (if necessary) constitutes your certified precinct returns.  Because this 
report will be c onsidered the precinct returns, the presiding judge must sign the report to certify its 
accuracy. 
 
Overvotes and Undervotes 
The CCS must also produce a tabulation of overvotes and undervotes by office and proposition and by 
election precinct. Most tabulation devices do this automatically as part of the precinct-by-precinct report. 
If your system does not automatically report this information, the manager will have to provide a record 
of this information by hand. 
 
Returns for Provisional, Corrective Action, and Late-Arriving Mail Ballots 
If the CCS reconvenes after election day for the counting of provisional, corrective action, and late-arriving 
mail ballots, new precinct returns and new unofficial results must be prepared with the aggregated totals 
from early voting, election day, and these provisional, corrective action, and late-arriving mail ballots. 
Additionally, the manager must prepare a certification and attach it to the returns (the precinct- by-
precinct report). The new unofficial election results can serve as this certification, provided that the 
manager signs and dates the results report. The SOS recommends that the CCS manager write a statement 
on the report indicating that these new unofficial election results supersede any previous reports 
previously printed by the CCS. The CCS manager should then place the certification and returns in 
Envelope #1 to be delivered to the presiding officer of the canvassing board. 
 
[Secs. 127.1301, 127.131; 1 TAC 81.37] 
 
ANNOUNCING UNOFFICIAL RESULTS 
Generally, the unofficial election results must be released as soon as they are available after the polls 
close. Alternatively, the presiding judge, in cooperation with the county election officer, may withhold the 
release of unofficial results until the last voter has voted. If you are using a voting system’s certified 
software to assist you with the accumulation and printing of reports, the printed summary report that has 
been adjusted to include any hand-counted ballots (if necessary) should be generated and should be used 
to report the unofficial results alongside the precinct-by-precinct report. 
 
[Sec. 127.1311] 
 
54 
REPORTING UNOFFICIAL RESULTS TO SOS 
In a special election ordered by the governor, a primary election, or the general election for state and 
county officers, the general custodian of election records is required to report unofficial results on election 
night to the SOS using the statewide vo ter registration and election management system.  The reporting 
of unofficial results to our office is a duty that is performed by the general custodian of election records 
or the custodian’s designee. While the custodian may designate an individual who is also serving in a role 
at the CCS to perform this duty, it is not required that the designee be appointed to a role in the CCS. The 
designated individual must have access to the statewide voter registration and election management 
system and must have completed the required security training.  
 
While this reporting process can occur in the CCS as part of CCS activities, it is not required to be conducted 
in the CCS. If the reporting process is conducted in the CCS , then poll watchers are entitled to  observe 
those activities. If the reporting process is conducted in the general custodian’s office and is not conducted 
in the CCS, then the general custodian is not required to provide poll watchers with access to their office 
if it is located outside of the CCS area.  
 
[Secs. 33.055, 33.056, 68.001, 68.034] 
 
PRINTING OF AUDIT LOGS 
An audit log produced by a central accumulator is considered part of the election records and is available 
for public inspection. In addition, a poll watcher may request copies of those audit logs at three different 
points while the CCS is convened and conducting counting activities: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
After the CCS personnel have completed the tabulation process, the CCS manager is required to print a 
copy of the entire audit log from the central accumulator, which must be retained with the other records 
from that election. Additionally, for counties with a population of 250,000 or more, the CCS manager and 
presiding judge must ensure that the audit logs are delivered to the SOS no later than the fifth day after 
vote counting is complete for the election. The SOS recommends that you plan for audit log requests and 
identify how you will respond to them as part of your CCS plan.  
 
[Sec. 127.009; 1 TAC 81.62]

55 
RECONCILIATION OF VOTE TOTALS 
General Reconciliation Procedures 
Reconciliation compares total ballots cast and spoiled ballots with the number of voters who checked in 
at a polling place. While minor variations may occur due to undervotes, fleeing voters, or other isolated 
occurrences, these figures should closely align. This process allows the authority  conducting the election 
to identify and resolve discrepancies before tabulation concludes and the CCS adjourns. If a major 
discrepancy is identified, the CCS presiding judge—in cooperation with the CCS manager and tabul ation 
supervisor—must investigate the cause. The presiding judge is then responsible for documenting the 
cause of the discrepancy and the specific steps taken to resolve it. 
 
Early Voting in Person 
To reconcile the results for early voting in person, the C CS presiding judge  should compare the total 
number of voters that checked  in on the combination forms or ePollbook, as applicable, to the total 
number of ballots cast and spoiled ballots. If there is a discrepancy in these figures, the presiding judge  
may need to contact the early voting clerk or deputy early voting clerks who supervised the various early 
voting locations to investigate and resolve the discrepancy. 
 
 
Early Voting by Mail 
To reconcile the results for early voting by mail, the CCS presiding judge should compare the number of 
ballots entered on the  Ballot Transmittal Form for Early Voted Ballots  (Form 10-6) from the EVBB to the 
number of ballots counted.  If there is a discrepancy in these figures, the presiding judge  may need to 
contact the EVBB presiding judge to investigate and resolve the discrepancy. 
 
Election Day 
To reconcile the results for election day, the CCS presiding judge should compare the number of voters 
that signed in on the combination forms or ePollbook, as applicable, to the total number of ballots cast 
on election day.  If there is a discrepancy in these figures, the presiding judge  may need to contact a 
presiding election judge to investigate and resolve the discrepancy. 
 
Final Reconciliation 
To reconcile the total results for the election after the CCS  has completed the final tabulation of results 
after election day, the presiding judge should compare the total number of voters who are listed as having 
voted in the election on the combination form or on the ePollbook and the number of ballots listed on 
the ballot transmittal form to the total number of votes cast during early voting in person, ballot by mail, 
and election day. Additionally, the presiding judge should compare the total number of registered voters 
in the territory to the total number of votes. Any discrepancies should be investigated and resolved prior 
to the canvass for the election and the release of the final results.

56 
 
Resolving Discrepancies 
If a discrepancy is found during any reconciliation, the CCS presiding judge—in cooperation with the CCS 
manager and tabulation supervisor —must determine if further investigation is required to identify the 
cause of the discrepancy and resolve it. This may involve collaborating with the EVBB or presiding election 
judges. Once the cause of the discrepancy is identified, the presiding judge must document the cause of 
the discrepancy and the specific steps taken to resolve it. For major discrepancies, the CCS may contact 
the SOS for additional guidance. 
 
Best Practice: The authority conducting the election should require each presiding election judge to 
reconcile the total ballots cast at the polling place against the total number of voters that signed in on the 
combination forms or ePollbook, as applicable. Providing this detailed documentation to CCS personnel is 
essential for resolving discrepancies efficiently during the reconciliation process. 
 
[Secs. 87.021, 87.1221, 127.007(b)] 
 
Reconciliation Forms–Election Night and Canvass Totals 
The presiding judge must provide and attest to a written reconciliation of votes and voters two times:  
• Preliminary Election Reconciliation Form  (Form 12-1)—Completed at the close of tabulation on 
election night before the CCS adjourns. This form reconciles the unofficial election night totals 
against the number of voters.  
• Election Reconciliation - Official Totals (Form 12-2)—Completed before the CCS concludes its final 
meeting for the election. This form reconciles the final totals —including late-arriving ballots by 
mail, corrective action ballots that were cured after election day and provisional ballots—that will 
be presented to the canvassing authority. 
 
Posting Requirements 
Both forms must be posted on the entity’s website on the same webpage as the election returns and 
results for that election . The webpage must be accessible without making more than two selections or 
viewing more than two network locations from the homepage. 
 
[Sec. 127.131] 
 
Secure Delivery and Transfer of Records 
The presiding judge must ensure all election materials —including voted ballots, poll lists, tally lists (if 
applicable), and zero reports —are placed in secure containers. To prevent unauthorized access, these 
containers must be sealed and their seal numbers recorded on the appropriate seal log. The process 
concludes once all containers and election records are delivered to the general custodian of election 
records. This transfer of custody formally ends the operational duties of the CCS. 
 
[Sec. 127.132] 
 
 
57 
Post-Election Reconciliation 
The general custodian must prepare a Reconciliation of Total Votes Cast at Each Polling Location  (Form 
12-3) that compares the total number of votes cast at each polling place to the total number of voters 
who were accepted to vote at that polling place.  This process applies to each early voting location and 
each election day polling place. The form mu st be completed no later than the 30th day after election 
day. The general custodian must post the completed form on the county’s website in the same location 
as the election results.  
 
[Sec. 66.005]

Chapter 9 
 
SECURITY REQUIREMENTS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

 
62 
The Election Code outlines security requirement s for all electronic voting system equipment and 
electronic media, which apply directly to equipment used or stored at the CCS. To ensure compliance and 
maintain a secure environment, the CCS manager and presiding judge may establish specific procedures 
to address specific conduct at the CCS. This section addresses those security requirements, as well as some 
common issues that may arise. 
 
VOTING SYSTEM SOFTWARE AND EQUIPMENT SECURITY 
REQUIREMENTS 
The sole purpose of voting system equipment is the conduct of an election, and only software certified by 
the SOS and necessary for an election may be loaded on the equipment. The computer on which you are 
performing your tabulation or accumulation of election totals is prohibited from running any other 
software. The tabulation computer itself, like other types of voting system equipment, may not be 
connected to any type of external communications network, including the internet. 
 
Accordingly, the general custodian of election records must ensure that there is no modem access to 
tabulating equipment. However, the SOS may prescribe procedures for transmission of unofficial results 
using equipment that is fully isolated from the tabulating equipment that is used to generate the official 
results, as outlined in Secretary of State Advisory No. 2019-23  – Electronic Voting System Procedures 
Advisory. 
 
The general custodian of election records must maintain the security of access control keys or passwords. 
This includes limiting who has administrative access to the tabulation software when it is in use at the 
CCS, and monitoring when those individuals have physical access to the equipment before, during, and 
after the CCS has convened. Furthermore, voting system equipment must be stored in a locked room.  
 
Security seals must be placed on each unit of voting system equipment to prevent unauthorized access. 
The general custodian of election records must establish a procedure for documenting which seals are 
placed on each piece of equipment and documenting any  instances where seals are removed; this 
documentation must include the identity of the person removing the seals and the purpose for doing so. 
Additionally, the tabulation supervisor is required to protect the program and equipment from tampering 
and unauthorized use. 
 
TRANSPORT, CHAIN OF CUSTODY , AND CONTINGENCY PLANNING 
The general custodian of election records must create a procedure for tracking the custody of voting 
system equipment once election parameters are loaded. The general custodian of electio n records must 
also adopt procedures for securely storing and transporting voting system equipment, including 
provisions for locations outside their direct control, such as overnight storage at a polling place. 
Procedures relating to the chain of custody must require two or more individuals to perform a check and 
verification check whenever a transfer of custody occurs, and the  general custodian of election records  
must create a training plan for relevant election officials that addresses these procedures. 
 
  
 
63 
For emergency management, the general custodian of election records must create a contingency plan 
for addressing voting machine failure, which must include timely notification to the SOS. A recovery plan 
must also be created to be followed if a breach in security procedures is indicated, requiring immediate 
notification to the SOS. Finally, for counties with a population of 250,000 or more, the CCS manager and 
presiding judge must ensure that the audit logs are delivered to the SOS no later than the fif th day after 
vote counting is complete for the election. 
 
ELECTRONIC MEDIA SECURITY REQUIREMENTS 
The general custodian of election records must create and maintain an inventory of all electronic media, 
which must include information about the polling locat ion where each piece of electronic media will be 
used. All electronic media must have a permanent label on the outside with a unique ID, such as a serial 
number or a specific code of letters and numbers, which can be either etched or printed on a tamper -
resistant label. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The general custodian of election records must also develop a procedure for tracking custody of electronic 
media from its storage location, through election coding and the election process, to its final post-election 
disposition and return to storage. This chain of custody requires two or more individuals to perform a 
check and verification check whenever a transfer of custody occurs. 
 
All election information storage media must be kept in the presence of an election official or in a secured 
location. No unauthorized individuals (including poll watchers) should ever be left unattended with voting 
system equipment, tabulation software, or voted ballots. To support this, the general custodian of 
election records must create and maint ain a secured location for storing the electronic information 
storage media when not in use, for coding a medium for an election, for transferring and installing the 
medium into the voting system equipment, and for storing the voting system equipment once the election 
parameters are loaded.  
 
Lastly, an authority operating a CCS may only purchase or use a ballot scan system if the system is only 
capable of using a data transfer media device that, once a cast vote record is written, is incapable of being 
modified without automatic detection of the modification and automatic rejection of the cast vote record. 
The system may not allow for this automatic detection and rejection process to be overridden or 
circumvented.  
  

 
64 
VOTING SYSTEM PERSONNEL SECURITY REQUIREMENTS 
The general custodian of election records is required to conduct a criminal background check for relevant 
election officials, staff, and temporary workers who are engaged in pre -election programming, testing, 
and preparing of the voting system equipment for early voting and election day. This does not include poll 
workers (election judges and clerks) assigned to work election voting centers or precincts, but does 
include temporary workers hired to test, store, or service voting equipment. Additionally, this includes all 
individuals who participate in the Public Logic and Accuracy Test and First Test of the Automatic Tabulating 
Equipment. 
 
[Secs. 123.034, 127.009, 127.123, 127.1231, 127.1301, 129.051, 129.052, 129.053, 129.054, 129.055, 
129.056] 
 
LICENSED PEACE OFFICER REQUIRED 
To ensure the security of ballot boxes containing voted ballots, the general custodian of election records 
must post a licensed peace officer at the CCS throughout the period 
of tabulation. This officer must be present when ever the CCS is 
officially convened, which includes counting before election day (in 
a county with a population of 100,000 or more), as well as after 
election day to count provisional, late -arriving, and/or corrective 
action mail ballots. 
 
However, a licensed peace officer is not required to be posted 
during periods when the CCS is not convened ; nor does this 
requirement extend to the EVBB, SVC, or any location other than 
the CCS itself. The individual appointed to this role must be currently 
licensed as a peace officer by the Texas Commission on Law 
Enforcement. Law enforcement agencies should refer to the Law 
Enforcement Guide for additional details and operational protocols. 
 
 [Sec. 127.1232]  
 
VIDEO SURVEILLANCE AND LIVESTREAM REQUIREMENTS  
In counties with a population of 100,000 or more, the general custodian of election records must maintain 
a video surveillance system and  a continuous livestream of all areas containing voted ballots. The scope 
of this requirement is outlined below, based on March 2026 data released by both the U.S. Census Bureau 
and the Texas Demographic Center:

Note: While the population rule currently applies to only 43 counties  (roughly one-sixth of the state ), 
these areas represent upwards of 86% of all potential voters in Texas. For the CCS and EVBB, this ensures 
the vast majority of voted ballots across the state are maintained under continuous livestream. 
 
Timeframe and Scope 
The livestream must begin from the time voted ballots are delivered to the SVC, EVBB, or CCS—whichever 
occurs first—and must remain continuous  until the local canvass of election results . At a minimum, the 
recording must capture all areas where ballots or media are: 
• Qualified (meeting places of the SVC or EVBB); 
• Processed or counted (within the CCS); and 
• Secured until the conclusion of the local canvass. 
 
Preservation Period and Public Inspection 
Once the canvass is complete, the video recordings become election records. The general custodian of 
election records must maintain these recordings for the duration of the 22-month preservation period for 
that election . These recordings are available for public inspection; however, the general custodian of 
election records must safeguard the election records throughout the inspection process. 
 
Ballots in Transit 
The livestream must capture all voted ballots (including paper and electronic media containing cast vote 
records) as they are processed, counted, or stored. This includes movement through hallways or other 
office areas. The general custodian of election records may satisfy this requirement via: 
• Mobile Coverage—Using a handheld or moving camera to follow the ballots. 
• Stationary Coverage—Utilizing a sequence of fixed cameras along the travel path. 
 
Note: If technical or environmental limitations prevent continuous recording during transit, the general 
custodian of election records  must permit poll watchers to accompany or witness the transfer  process. 
The absence of a watcher does not prevent or delay the transfer of materials. 
 
System Integrity and Security Protocols 
While livestreaming is mandatory for covered entities, each entity running the election has the discretion 
to design its own setup. Refer to the Video Surveillance Recommendations  for best practices on 
implementation and evaluation. 
• Camera Placement: When processing or storing ballots in a building that also functions as a polling 
place, or
ient cameras to ensure no polling activity is captured. While the Election Code does not 
mandate a specific number of cameras, the setup must provide a clear, unobstructed view of all 
required areas. 
 
66 
• Visual Clarity: While specific resolution or requirement to capture specific individual tasks is not 
mandated, visibility must be sufficient to ensure transparency of all handling and storage 
processes. 
• Audio: A video record is mandatory, but audio recording is not required. 
• Hosting and Public Access:  Entities may 
choose their own hosting platform, but 
the livestream must be publicly 
accessible at no cost to the viewer via a 
direct link on the county’s website. 
• Network Security: The general 
custodian of election records  should 
work with the county’s IT department to 
establish robust cybersecurity 
measures. Consider using a secondary 
network to host and transmit the feed to 
isolate livestream traffic from the 
county’s primary internal network. 
 
[Secs. 1.012(b), 61.014, 66.058, 87.026 127.1232, 127.1311] 
 
WIRELESS COMMUNICATION DEVICES 
The CCS manager maintains responsibility for the administration of the CCS  and the supervision of its 
personnel. Under this authority, the CCS manager may establish specific procedures governing the use of 
wireless communication devic es. Our office recommends that these procedures be specifically listed in 
the CCS plan. Because CCS activities often begin before the polls close on election day, established written 
procedures are vital to prevent the premature release of election results . Unauthorized disclosure of 
results before the close of polls or before the last voter has cast a ballot is a violation of Section 61.007. 
 
A poll watcher possessing any device capable of recording images or sound may not be accepted for 
service unless th ey agree to disable or deactivate the device. The presiding judge has the authority to 
inquire whether a watcher is in possession of any prohibited recording device before accepting the 
watcher for service.  
 
The CCS manager may implement a policy prohibit ing the use of wireless communication devices within 
the CCS, except when used  by the manager, tabulation supervisor, presiding judge, state inspector, or 
voting system technician  in the performance of their official duties . If this policy is adopted, all other 
personnel must be instructed to deactivate their devices upon entry. Any individual wishing to use a device 
should obtain permission from the presiding judge to leave the CCS before using said device.  
 
[Secs. 33.051(c), 33.055(b), 61.007, 127.002, 127.007]

Chapter 10 
 
POLL WATCHERS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
  

68 
A poll watcher serving at a CC S may be present at any time the station is open for the purpose of 
processing or preparing to process election results until the election officers complete their duties at the 
station. This section addresses the authority and rights of poll watchers at the CCS and the procedures for 
the acceptance of watchers. 
ACCEPTANCE AND QUALIFICATION 
A poll watcher who is appointed to serve must present a valid Certificate of Appointment of Poll Watcher 
(Form 4-26, 4-27, 4-28, or 4-29) and Certificate of Completion of Poll Watcher Training administered by 
the SOS to the CCS presiding judge when the watcher reports for service. The certificates provided by the 
watcher must be retained with the records of the CCS . The presiding judge must require the watcher to 
countersign the Certificate of Appointment of Poll Watcher to ensure that the watcher is the same person 
who signed the Certificate of Appointment of Poll Watcher. 
A watcher may not be accepted for service if the watcher has possession of a device capable of recording 
images or sound unless the watcher agrees to disable or deacti vate the device. The CCS presiding judge 
may inquire whether a watcher has possession of any prohibited recording device before accepting the 
watcher for service. 
A watcher who presents himself or herself with the required certificates at the proper time must be 
accepted for service unless the person is ineligible to serve, the watcher refuses to disable or deactivate 
a prohibited recording device, or the number of watchers to which the appointing authority is entitled 
have already been accepted. If the watcher is not accepted for service, the certificates must be returned 
to the watcher with a signed, written statement of the reason for the rejection.

“I swear (or affirm) that I will not disrupt the voting process or harass voters in the 
discharge of my duties.”  
 
Identification 
If the watcher is accepted for service, an election officer will provide the watcher with a form of 
identification that must be worn by the watcher in the CCS.4

[Secs. 33.055, 33.056, 33.058, 33.061; 1 TAC 81.62] 
 
DISRUPTIONS IN THE CCS 
While a poll watcher is entitled to observe any activity conducted at the location the watcher is serving, 
they must not disrupt the qualifying process. The CCS presiding judge is responsible for maintaining order, 
preventing breaches of the peace, and preventing Election Code violations while the CCS  is convened, 
possessing the same authority as a district judge to perform these duties. If a poll watcher is disruptive, 
impedes the ability of personnel performing their duties, or willfully violates the Election Code, the 
presiding judge may remove the watcher from the CCS. 
 
[Secs. 32.075, 127.005] 
 
OBSERVING DELIVERY OF BALLOTS, RECORDS, AND MEDIA 
A poll watcher accepted for service at a polling place is entitled to follow the transfer of election materials 
from the polling place at which the watcher was accepted to a regional substation, CCS , or any other 
location designated to process election materials. If a poll watcher who was appointed to serve at a polling 
place will be also serving as a poll watcher at the EVBB or CCS, the watcher will need to present a new 
certificate of appointment and certificate of completion of poll watcher training administered by the SOS 
to the respective presiding judge. 
 
[Secs. 33.060, 33.0605] 
 
 
 
 
71 
OBSERVING THE CENTRAL COMPUTER USED FOR TABULATION 
A poll watcher must be permitted to observe any activity occurring at the location at which the watcher 
is serving, including the activities performed in the room in which the tabulation computer is located. In 
some counties, the CCS  or the portion of the CCS  that contains the computer used to accu mulate vote 
totals and generate reports will be located in a small area.  Poll watchers must be provided access to this 
area.  
 
If the location is not large enough to accommodate all poll watchers desiring access, the SOS recommends 
that the CCS manager establish a rotation system to allow all poll watchers serving at the location to have 
an opportunity to observe the activities occurring in the tabulation room.  The rotation system should 
allow for watchers of opposing interests to serve simultaneously and allow for equal observation time for 
all watchers who wish to observe the activities occurring in that room.  Any procedures established to 
implement this process should be included in the written plan for the CCS. 
 
[Sec. 33.056]
